The Portuguese Pavilion to Invite Four African Countries Through "Hands on the Ground" at the 2027 Venice Architecture Biennale

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1217 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Archdaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Portuguese Directorate-General for the Arts announced on November 16 the curatorial proposal that will represent the country at the 20th International Architecture Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia in 2027.
  • In a recent development, the Portuguese Directorate-General for the Arts announced on November 16 the curatorial proposal that will represent the country at the 20th International Architecture Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia in 2027.
  • "Hands on the Ground" invites Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique and São Tomé and Príncipe, countries without permanent representation at the Biennale, to the Portuguese Pavilion.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Portuguese Directorate-General for the Arts announced on November 16 the curatorial proposal that will represent the country at the 20th International Architecture Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia in 2027. The selected project was "Mãos ao Chão (Hands on the Ground)," an artistic and curatorial proposal by Joanna Alice Helm, Remígio van Eys Chilaule and Samuel de Brito Gonçalves. It was chosen from a limited competition among three teams. The other two proposals were "Analog Twins" by Alice Clanet-Hallard, Edgar Brito, Francisco Lobo and Romea Mury, and "Matéria Viva — Os materiais da construção portuguesa e o saber que resiste" by Helena Botelho. The evaluation committee was composed of Álvaro Domingues, Andreia Garcia, João Gomes da Silva, Mariana Pestana and Tânia Teixeira.

In a recent development, the Portuguese Directorate-General for the Arts announced on November 16 the curatorial proposal that will represent the country at the 20th International Architecture Exhibition – La Biennale di Venezia in 2027. The selected project was "Mãos ao Chão (Hands on the Ground)," an artistic and curatorial proposal by Joanna Alice Helm, Remígio van Eys Chilaule and Samuel de Brito Gonçalves. It was chosen from a limited competition among three teams. The other two proposals were "Analog Twins" by Alice Clanet-Hallard, Edgar Brito, Francisco Lobo and Romea Mury, and "Matéria Viva — Os materiais da construção portuguesa e o saber que resiste" by Helena Botelho. The evaluation committee was composed of Álvaro Domingues, Andreia Garcia, João Gomes da Silva, Mariana Pestana and Tânia Teixeira.

"Hands on the Ground" invites Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique and São Tomé and Príncipe, countries without permanent representation at the Biennale, to the Portuguese Pavilion. The four countries are former Portuguese colonies that now maintain close diplomatic, cultural and economic ties with Portugal. Portugal established trading posts, settlements and colonies across these territories starting in the 15th century and exercised administrative authority over them until their independence in the 1970s. Together with Angola, the four form the PALOP (Países Africanos de Língua Oficial Portuguesa), and all five belong to the Community of Portuguese Language Countries (CPLP).

The invitation draws on a Finnish gesture from 1976, when Finland ceded its space to showcase Portuguese architectural knowledge. Unlike other European countries, Portugal does not have a permanent national pavilion building. Its exhibition will be hosted at Fondaco Marcello, a 15th-century building on the Grand Canal, which also hosted the Portuguese exhibition at the 19th Venice Architecture Biennale in 2025. "Hands on the Ground" proposes to include the African countries as "a source of learning, not a distant object." The curatorial approach organizes content into six overarching themes: extreme climates, local materials, passive responses, memory and innovation, ways of doing, and toward building the future. Local authors are invited to develop critical manifestos on these topics in different formats.

The Portuguese exhibition will therefore present voices from the former colonies to bring forward local building knowledge and establish a dialogue with critical and interpretive records that connect their experiences to the foundations of the Venice Biennale. The curatorial theme of the 20th edition, by Wang Shu and Lu Wenyu, is "Do Architecture — For the Possibility of Coexistence Facing a Real Reality." It calls for a return to the material act of doing architecture, from a critical perspective on the contemporary disconnection between the discipline and lived reality. The curators of the Portuguese pavilion see this invitation as an opportunity to present architecture as an act of making that brings together earth, craftsmanship, memory and innovation, and highlights the effort to preserve cultural heritage.

After the Biennale, the exhibition is expected to tour Portugal, Cabo Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mozambique and São Tomé and Príncipe. The United States' contribution to the upcoming edition will also highlight craftsmanship and makers through "Earth Craft," an exhibition on the country's architecture in earth in its many forms: brick, rammed earth, adobe and concrete masonry. The Nordic exhibition, housed in Sverre Fehn's modern pavilion, is titled "Painted Matter" and will explore the role of traditional decorative painting techniques in contemporary architecture. The Swiss pavilion will explore water as a territorial, ecological and political condition, taking Switzerland's role as "Europe's water tower" as its conceptual point of departure, while the Icelandic pavilion will examine bathing culture through the lens of architecture, public space and social interaction.

The private house in Kaklebi, near Tbilisi, is composed of a series of timber-clad volumes rather than a single block, arranged to follow the slope of a wooded site and to preserve its existing mature trees. Distributed across multiple levels, the building reduces its own visual presence in the landscape while giving each level a distinct relationship to the terrain below.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that the 31st United Nations Climate Change Conference (COP31) concluded on November 22, 2026, in Antalya, Türkiye, following negotiations that extended beyond the scheduled closing date. Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading the negotiations, the summit brought together representatives of nearly 200 Parties, alongside researchers, businesses, climate organizations, and civil society, to advance international climate action. While countries reached decisions on climate finance, adaptation, just transition, and other agenda items, they failed to agree on the proposed overarching Antalya Pact, with disagreements over fossil fuels, finance, and the level of ambition in the final text. For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

Hosted by Türkiye with Australia leading the negotiations, the summit brought together representatives of nearly 200 Parties, alongside researchers, businesses, climate organizations, and civil society, to advance international climate action. While countries reached decisions on climate finance, adaptation, just transition, and other agenda items, they failed to agree on the proposed overarching Antalya Pact, with disagreements over fossil fuels, finance, and the level of ambition in the final text. For the built environment, COP31 advanced several initiatives addressing building energy performance, electrification, urban resilience, and climate investment, while leaving broader questions of implementation and international coordination unresolved.

Buildings and construction remain central to climate action, accounting for a significant share of global energy consumption and emissions while also being exposed to rising temperatures, flooding, and other climate-related risks. At COP31, the Turkish Presidency introduced the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, a voluntary framework targeting a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock by 2035, compared with 2020 levels. Discussions on urban resilience also addressed the relationship between national climate commitments and investment at the local level, particularly in housing, infrastructure, and adaptation. While these initiatives provide frameworks for further action, their implementation will depend on national policies, financing, and coordination across public and private sectors.

Below are four developments from COP31 relevant to architecture, cities, and the built environment.

The Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings.

One of COP31's most direct initiatives for the building sector was the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, launched by the Turkish Presidency on October 29 in collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)-hosted Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction (GlobalABC). The voluntary framework supports two of the Presidency's 2035 objectives: pursuing a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock compared with 2020 levels, and accelerating efficient electrification in buildings in support of the 35-by-35 target, which seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. At the second ministerial meeting of the Intergovernmental Council for Buildings and Climate (ICBC), held during COP31, 24 countries, the European Commission, and 38 non-Party stakeholders expressed support for or endorsed the Compact.

One of COP31's most direct initiatives for the building sector was the Antalya Compact for Energy Efficient Buildings, introduced by the Turkish Presidency on October 29 in collaboration with the United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP)-hosted Global Alliance for Buildings and Construction (GlobalABC). The voluntary framework supports two of the Presidency's 2035 objectives: pursuing a 25% reduction in the operational energy intensity of the global building stock compared with 2020 levels, and accelerating efficient electrification in buildings in support of the 35-by-35 target, which seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. At the second ministerial meeting of the Intergovernmental Council for Buildings and Climate (ICBC), held during COP31, 24 countries, the European Commission, and 38 non-Party stakeholders expressed support for or endorsed the Compact.

The framework identifies six areas for action, including integrating energy efficiency and electrification into national strategies, strengthening building energy and carbon performance, accelerating renovation of existing buildings, reducing energy demand, improving buildings' flexibility within energy systems, and mobilizing finance and technical capacity. Its proposed measures range from stronger building energy codes and renovation strategies to electrified heating and cooling, energy management, passive cooling, and investment in public buildings and social infrastructure. While the Compact does not establish binding targets for individual countries, it provides a shared framework for governments and industry to advance building decarbonization, linking operational energy performance with renovation, affordability, and long-term resilience.

Climate-Resilient Cities: Housing, Infrastructure, and Local Implementation.

According to recent reports, cities and urban resilience were also prominent at COP31, with the Turkish Presidency and UN-Habitat convening a High-Level Dialogue on Urban Resilience, Adaptation and Climate Action on November 12. The discussions addressed how national climate intends and adaptation strategies can be translated into investments at the local level, with housing, infrastructure, urban regeneration, informal settlement upgrading, and post-disaster reconstruction identified as areas requiring stronger implementation. Participants emphasized the importance of connecting national climate commitments with local development priorities while strengthening coordination between governments, municipalities, financial institutions, and development partners. The dialogue also highlighted the financing gap facing cities, with climate-resilient infrastructure and services requiring investment beyond current levels.

The discussions positioned housing and basic urban services as part of climate adaptation, highlighting the need for homes that can withstand floods and extreme heat, infrastructure that can continue functioning during climate-related disasters, and urban development strategies that address the needs of vulnerable communities. Rather than treating resilience as a separate technical objective, the discussions linked it to housing conditions, public services, reconstruction processes, and the capacity of cities to respond to climate risks. The emphasis on implementation also highlighted the challenges of moving from planning to investment, particularly for municipalities that lack the financial or technical capacity to develop large-scale climate projects.

Financing Urban Resilience Through the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility.

Alongside discussions on climate adaptation, COP31 highlighted the Sustainable Urban Resilience Financing Facility (SURFF), an initiative developed through Türkiye's İLBANK in partnership with UN-Habitat and the World Bank. Launched ahead of the summit during New York Climate Week, the initiative aims to help cities and countries translate climate commitments into investment-ready urban resilience projects, addressing the gap between national climate strategies and implementation at the municipal level. It is structured around three pillars: country-led Resilient Cities Platforms, a Resilient Cities Centre of Excellence, and an international dialogue intended to facilitate cooperation, share experience, and improve access to climate finance.

Its priorities include resilient infrastructure, climate adaptation, and projects that respond to the needs of cities and their communities. Rather than operating as a upcoming financing fund, the facility aims to connect cities with existing financing mechanisms, technical assistance, and implementation partners. Its effectiveness will therefore depend on the development of investment pipelines, the availability of finance, and the ability to translate its framework into financed and completed urban interventions.

Fossil Fuels and Electrification: An Unresolved Transition.

Industry observers note that the transition away from fossil fuels remained one of the most contested challenges at COP31. Countries were divided over whether the final political text should include an explicit commitment to move away from coal, oil, and gas. The proposed Antalya Pact did not include a clear reference to fossil fuels, prompting objections from the European Union, the United Kingdom, and several climate-vulnerable nations, which argued that the text did not adequately address the primary drivers of climate change. Disagreements over the language of the energy transition, climate finance, and the level of ambition required prevented the draft from reaching consensus. The outcome leaves the commitment made at COP28 to transition away from fossil fuels in energy systems without a new collective roadmap at COP31.

According to recent reports, outside the formal negotiations, efforts to advance electrification continued through voluntary initiatives. Around 80 countries supported the Presidency's 35-by-35 Global Electrification Pledge, which seeks to increase electricity's share of global final energy consumption to 35% by 2035. For the built environment, electrification connects the transition to buildings through heating, cooling, cooking, and energy systems, while energy efficiency and passive design strategies can reduce demand. The Antalya Compact similarly addresses building energy use through renovation, efficient systems, and measures to reduce operational demand. However, electrification targets and building efficiency initiatives do not replace a negotiated global commitment to phase out fossil fuels, leaving the pace of transition dependent on national policies, energy infrastructure, investment, and further international cooperation.

As countries continue to work toward the goals of the Paris Agreement, the outcomes of COP31 leave both sector-specific initiatives and broader climate negotiations to be carried forward. The next edition, COP32, is scheduled to take place in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia in 2027, where discussions are expected to continue around implementation, climate finance, energy transition, and adaptation, including how commitments can be translated into actions at the scale of buildings, infrastructure, and cities.

The Grand Terminal provides berths for two megaships, which can enjoy a variety of leisure and cultural amenities offered by the impressive waterside complex. Hassell Principal and Head of Design Ashley Munday remarked, "We are really excited that our Grand Terminal is beginning its life as a festival venue for the World Cup, but what excites us even more is its future as a loved piece of the city, embedded in the cultural fabric of Doha. It is a building that doesn't just have a singular function as a cruise terminal, but has been designed to absorb other uses during the year, like markets, exhibitions, and festivals. For us, this is a civic project that has to respond to many complex needs and requirements at once, but still has an 'outward' role to face the world and welcome people into a place that is really just emerging as a destination.".

Does Your Building Work or Does It Just Photograph Well? What Neuroscience and Use Data Could Teach Architects

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Architecture reaches people through whatever medium carries it, and each new medium changes our picture of what a good building looks like.
  • According to recent reports, architecture reaches people through whatever medium carries it, and each latest medium changes our picture of what a good building looks like.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Architecture reaches people through whatever medium carries it, and each new medium changes our picture of what a good building looks like. For example, when 3D modeling software arrived, the novelty of complex shapes drove the starchitecture era of the 2010s, and projects built on those experiments earned awards such as the Pritzker Prize. Today the medium is the social media feed. A building exists first as a model and then as a render, long before it exists as a place. Meanwhile, research in neuroarchitecture is building a different picture based on how people actually experience buildings. So how could those two seemingly unrelated topics close a loop that may lead to the profession's next creative frontier?

According to recent reports, architecture reaches people through whatever medium carries it, and each latest medium changes our picture of what a good building looks like. For example, when 3D modeling software arrived, the novelty of complex shapes drove the starchitecture era of the 2010s, and projects built on those experiments earned awards such as the Pritzker Prize. Today the medium is the social media feed. A building exists first as a model and then as a render, long before it exists as a place. Meanwhile, research in neuroarchitecture is building a different picture based on how people actually experience buildings. So how could those two seemingly unrelated topics close a loop that may lead to the profession's next creative frontier?

According to recent reports, in the book Cognitive Architecture, Ann Sussman and Justin Hollander examine how the brain reacts to the built environment. In their research, people looked at photographs of buildings while their eye movements were tracked. Viewers tended to skip blank, featureless facades but lingered on details, contrast, and other people. One case study, the Stapleton Library in New York, shows how much fenestration patterns matter: windows provide areas of contrast that the eye seeks out and stays with. Their study suggests that architecture tuned to these cues could serve its occupants at a layer deeper than aesthetics. Sussman's broader argument is that the brain works at walking speed and eye level, hunting for faces, contrast, and activity at the ground floor.

In the book Cognitive Architecture, Ann Sussman and Justin Hollander examine how the brain reacts to the built environment. In their research, people looked at photographs of buildings while their eye movements were tracked. Viewers tended to skip blank, featureless facades but lingered on details, contrast, and other people. One case study, the Stapleton Library in Fresh York, demonstrates how much fenestration patterns matter: windows provide areas of contrast that the eye seeks out and stays with. Their study suggests that architecture tuned to these cues could serve its occupants at a layer deeper than aesthetics. Sussman's broader argument is that the brain works at walking speed and eye level, hunting for faces, contrast, and activity at the ground floor.

Industry observers note that anjan Chatterjee's lab at the University of Pennsylvania adds nuance to this picture. They summarize architectural experience in three elements: coherence, or how organized and legible a space is; fascination, or how rich in information an environment is; and hominess, or how comfortable it feels. Everyone weighs these differently, but people with an architectural background seem to give coherence more weight than non-architects do. At the same time, he also makes a second point: architects often predict how a building will work, but they rarely collect post-occupancy information to test those predictions.

Related Article Scroll & Stroll: How Social Media Is Rewriting Architectural Cultural Tourism.

However, these days, a building lives first as a render, which later gets transferred to a tech giant's social media feed. That matters a lot, because a legible, coherent silhouette that grabs attention is often what the algorithms reward. In some cases, this might even put the architectural brief at risk of becoming a framing exercise: a legible silhouette, a dramatic angle, a frontal moment that survives a person's attention span. In fact, a study of Instagram posts from the Technical University of Munich suggests that architecture is increasingly interacting with social media platforms and, in doing so, taking on their trends and logic. Interestingly, the authors also conclude that spectacle alone does not sustain public interest; popularity is also maintained through function, which depends on repeated documentation of the building's use.

Sources indicate that in that sense, the city of Venice in Italy offers an early case study. Photographs of Calatrava's glass-and-steel Ponte della Costituzione are beautiful, but its glass steps proved slippery in the rain, causing people to fall. Finally, years of complaints led the city to consider replacing the glass with stone. The failure was physical rather than perceptual, but it shows the same gap: the picture and the place were judged by different tests, and only one of them was being taken into account before the bridge was built.

Finally, years of complaints led the city to consider replacing the glass with stone. The failure was physical rather than perceptual, but it indicates the same gap: the picture and the place were judged by different tests, and only one of them was being taken into account before the bridge was built.

That is the dichotomy that architecture tends to fall into: the "money shot" is taken from far away, standing still, usually with a few people around. The brain, as Sussman describes it, works at walking speed and eye level. The gap, in that sense, seems to be a missing feedback loop. Researchers at the Technical University of Denmark describe a performance gap between how buildings are expected to perform and how they actually do; in one of their studies, desk sensors indicated that an assumed 100 percent occupancy during design was closer to 70 percent in practice. This is the post-occupancy problem Chatterjee describes: predictions are made, but rarely tested.

Researchers at the Technical University of Denmark describe a performance gap between how buildings are expected to perform and how they actually do; in one of their studies, desk sensors showed that an assumed 100 percent occupancy during design was closer to 70 percent in practice. This is the post-occupancy problem Chatterjee describes: predictions are made, but rarely tested.

The tools architects use in their everyday work should close this gap, but they are not able to just yet. BIM software, for example, works like a giant spreadsheet: a database of walls, doors, and quantities that happens to have a 3D view. Dave Lemont, who led Revit's technology before Autodesk acquired it, explained in an ArchDaily interview that moving a wall updates every proposal, section, and schedule, while changing a material often sends the team back to specifications, spreadsheets, and drawings, which are changed by hand. But the underlying common ground in this topic is not fragmentation, but rather that the model records what was intended, not what happened after construction.

It has been revealed that the tools architects use in their everyday work should close this gap, but they are not able to just yet. BIM software, for example, works like a giant spreadsheet: a database of walls, doors, and quantities that happens to have a 3D view. Dave Lemont, who led Revit's technology before Autodesk acquired it, explained in an ArchDaily interview that moving a wall updates every blueprint, section, and schedule, while changing a material often sends the team back to specifications, spreadsheets, and drawings, which are changed by hand. But the underlying common ground in this topic is not fragmentation, but rather that the model records what was intended, not what happened after construction.

According to recent reports, therefore, it is possible to see BIM as one more medium that represents a building, while the interesting part could be the shift from representing intent to recording use. Imagine adding the missing column to that spreadsheet: how the building is actually used. Temperature, daylight, noise, density, and anonymized demographics, from every building a firm completes. Because neuroscience is about perception, not just physical conditions, the column would pair those sensor readings with simple occupant feedback on how coherent, engaging, and comfortable a space feels, and with observations of where people actually linger. Over time, this could become a database of what worked, for whom, and in which climate and specific conditions. Architecture's next creative frontier may not be bolder forms, but a humbler habit: go back, measure, and let the building tell you what actually worked.

Global South Forum on ATHIS

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 15 min read (2922 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Archdaily

⏱️ ~15 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Heliópolis, one of the largest favelas in the city of São Paulo, will host an international gathering in defense of dignified housing from December 6 to 8.
  • Recent findings suggest that heliópolis, one of the largest favelas in the city of São Paulo, will host an international gathering in defense of dignified housing from December 6 to 8.
  • SERVICEGlobal South Forum on Technical Assistance for Social Interest Housing (ATHIS)When: December 6, 7, and 8, 2026Where: Instituto Baccarelli — Estrada das Lágrimas, No.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Read the original version in Portuguese here.

Heliópolis, one of the largest favelas in the city of São Paulo, will host an international gathering in defense of dignified housing from December 6 to 8. The Global South Forum on ATHIS will bring together representatives from governments, international bodies, universities, social movements, civil society organizations, and community leaders from countries across Latin America and Africa at the Instituto Baccarelli to discuss ways to strengthen social interest housing policies. The program includes technical visits to five territories in São Paulo on the 6th, followed by two days of debates on the 7th and 8th.The event is organized by the Council of Architecture and Urbanism of São Paulo (CAU/SP), the United Nations Human Settlements Programme (UN-Habitat), and the Brazilian Cooperation Agency of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs (ABC/MRE) as part of the project ATHIS en Rede: fortalecendo a moradia digna no Sul Global (ATHIS in Network: Strengthening Dignified Housing in the Global South). The initiative seeks to expand the exchange of experiences and strengthen cooperation between countries to advance the implementation of Technical Assistance for Social Interest Housing. Admission is free, and registration is available via the link https://www.forum.athisemrede.causp.gov.br/ "Addressing the housing crisis requires more than just increasing the supply of homes: we need integrated solutions, consistent public policies, and cooperation between different actors and countries, always considering the realities of each territory. The Global South Forum on ATHIS is an opportunity to bring experiences closer together, share knowledge, and strengthen joint paths to advance this agenda and turn the right to adequate housing into reality," explains Rayne Ferretti Moraes, head of UN-Habitat in Brazil.Program HighlightsThe opening ceremony on December 7 will feature representatives from UN-Habitat, CAU/SP, and ABC/MRE, as well as federal government authorities and representatives from state and municipal governments, international organizations, and partner institutions.The federal government will be represented by the Chief of Staff of the Presidency of the Republic, the Secretariat of Institutional Relations, and the Ministries of Cities; Foreign Affairs; Management and Innovation in Public Services; Agrarian Development and Family Farming; and Environment and Climate Change, in addition to the Caixa Econômica Federal. The agenda also includes representatives from the Government of the State of São Paulo and the City of São Paulo.The meeting will also host delegations and representatives from countries such as Cape Verde, Mozambique, South Africa, Mexico, Uruguay, Cuba, Ecuador, Peru, and Colombia, as well as representatives from the BRICS nations. This international participation will allow for a dialogue between experiences from different contexts and a discussion on ways to strengthen social interest housing policies."Countries in the Global South share significant challenges: rapid urbanization, socio-spatial inequalities, housing deficits, urban informality, and increasing exposure to climate risks. However, they also share something very valuable: experiences, knowledge, and solutions developed from their own realities through South-South Cooperation," highlights Mônica Salmito, Lead Analyst for the Brazil-UN Habitat Program at the ABC/MRE.Among the guests for the dialogue panels are prominent figures in the field of the right to housing and urban reform, such as Koldo Kasla, UN Special Rapporteur on the right to adequate housing; references in Brazilian urbanism such as Raquel Rolnik, Ermínia Maricato, and Nabil Bonduki; historical leaders of popular movements for housing and urban reform, such as Evaniza Rodrigues and Benedito Roberto Barbosa (Dito); as well as members of the Executive and Legislative branches, such as Ediane Maria, Luiza Erundina, Inês Magalhães, and José Police Neto. The program also includes representatives from the Landless Workers' Movement (MST), the João Pinheiro Foundation, and the Institute for Applied Economic Research (Ipea). The academic community will also have a significant presence, with representatives from universities in São Paulo, Paraíba, Santa Catarina, Bahia, Brasília, and Minas Gerais.Global South Charter and ATHIS in Network PlatformThe closing of the Forum on December 8 will feature the reading of the Global South Charter, a document containing recommendations and commitments developed throughout the debates. The ATHIS in Network Platform will also be introduced, serving as a permanent space for exchange and coordination among participating countries. On this occasion, the 2026 edition of the publication Vivenciando ATHIS, by CAU/SP, which presents projects fostered by the council throughout the year, will also be released.Exhibition Presents ATHIS ExperiencesIn addition to the debate panels, the Forum will feature the Vivenciando ATHIS Exhibition, which will showcase projects supported by CAU/SP and other national and international experiences related to housing improvement, urbanization, land regularization, and community strengthening. Through panels and presentations, the initiative aims to bring the public closer to solutions developed in different territories and will allow attendees to learn how technical assistance can contribute to improving housing conditions and strengthening communities. Technical Visits and Territorial ExperiencesOn December 6, the program will take place in five territories in São Paulo. Through simultaneous itineraries, participants will be able to see in practice the transformation promoted in communities through ATHIS. These include:Diadema: experiences in housing renovation and qualification carried out with technical assistance, developed by the Housing and Human Settlements Laboratory of FAU-USP (LabHab) and Peabiru Community and Environmental Works in partnership with the City of Diadema.Mauá: experiences that link housing, urban infrastructure, and adaptation to climate change, developed by UN-Habitat within the scope of the Periferia Viva Mauá project and the Pólis Institute. São Paulo - Jaraguá Neighborhood: experiences linking housing and sanitation in the Guarani indigenous territory of Tekoa Pyau. The activity addresses the implementation of sanitation solutions and their relationship with the ways of life, community organization, and cultural specificities of the Guarani territory, highlighting a technical assistance practice built in dialogue with the knowledge and needs of the community.São Paulo - City Center: housing experiences in occupations and tenements located in the central region of São Paulo, monitored by Fio Popular Technical Assistance. The visit will allow for an understanding of the processes of community organization, social production of habitat, and the promotion of the right to housing.Santos: experiences developed by the Elos Institute that link housing, community development, social inclusion, and food security. The visit will highlight approaches to strengthening vulnerable communities, showing how actions aimed at improving living conditions can contribute to building more resilient, healthy, and inclusive territories.Together, these itineraries demonstrate the different forms of ATHIS action and the importance of building solutions with communities, based on the needs of each territory.Why ATHIS?Technical Assistance for Social Interest Housing (ATHIS), guaranteed by Federal Law No. 11.888/2008, ensures that low-income families have free access to architecture and urbanism services for the construction, renovation, expansion, and regularization of their homes. The policy recognizes that dignified housing goes far beyond providing a roof: it involves structural safety, health, accessibility, comfort, infrastructure, and adequate territorial conditions.Despite its importance, the implementation of ATHIS still faces obstacles, such as a lack of budgetary resources, low institutionalization of the policy, and the limited technical capacity of many municipalities. "In this context, the exchange of experiences between countries and institutions can help identify solutions, strengthen local capacities, and expand the reach of public policies," states Camila Moreno de Camargo, president of CAU/SP.It is in this scenario that the ATHIS in Network project bets on South-South and Trilateral Cooperation as a strategy to bring together governments, professionals, universities, and social organizations, promoting the circulation of knowledge and experiences developed within the territories of the Global South itself. "More than just a meeting, the Forum intends to leave behind a legacy of coordination tools and commitments to advance the realization of the right to adequate housing," adds Camila.Heliópolis and the Instituto BaccarelliThe choice of the Instituto Baccarelli as the venue for the Forum goes beyond infrastructure: it translates the principles of ATHIS by showing that the right to dignified housing includes access to culture, education, and quality public facilities. "The Institute starts from the needs of the territory, values community leadership, and invests in permanent actions for social transformation. Holding the Forum within Heliópolis means debating dignified housing where housing challenges are experienced every day and where collective responses are also being built," notes Nilcio Regueira Dias, coordinator of the ATHIS in Network project for UN-Habitat.Founded in 1996, after a fire left families homeless in Heliópolis, the Institute was born from the initiative of maestro Silvio Baccarelli to provide music lessons to 36 children affected by the tragedy. Three decades later, about 1,650 students receive free musical training at the site. In addition to music, the Institute, which also distributes 3.5 tons of food per month to students and their families, maintains social and inclusion actions and manages public facilities in Heliópolis and other regions of São Paulo.

#182949. 7 Subtle Signs You’re Dating for Validation, Not Connection

📅 22 Apr 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1141 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Self ↗ Open Full Page

7 Subtle Signs You’re Dating for Validation, Not Connection

📅 22 Apr 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1141 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Self

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, for a long time, I thought I was doing everything right in dating.
  • In theory, I was putting myself out there: going on dates, meeting people, and staying open even when it felt exhausting.
  • But after what felt like an uncountable number of first dates in Upcoming York City, I started to notice a pattern: I treated dates like auditions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, for a long time, I thought I was doing everything right in dating. After getting out of an eight-year relationship—and then a rebound that emotionally wrecked me in ways I didn’t fully process for at least a couple years—I spent the next few years in a strange in-between.

In theory, I was putting myself out there: going on dates, meeting people, and staying open even when it felt exhausting. But in reality, it felt more like going through the motions, like I was playing a role I had gotten really good at. I had just enough distance to feel in control, but not enough awareness to realize how that distance was shaping my behavior.

But after what felt like an uncountable number of first dates in Upcoming York City, I started to notice a pattern: I treated dates like auditions. I would show up polished, engaged, and asking the right questions. If they liked me—texted after, complimented me, and wanted to see me again—I felt this immediate sense of relief, almost like I had passed a test. But that feeling rarely lasted, and more importantly, I almost never stopped to ask myself the most basic question: Did I even like them?

In a recent development, it took me a long time to realize that I wasn’t actually dating for connection—I was dating for validation. And according to therapists, that distinction can be subtle but significant, often showing up in patterns that feel normal on the surface but are actually rooted in the need to feel chosen rather than the desire to truly know someone.

Here are some red flags that indicate you might be seeking companionship for the wrong reasons, according to dating experts.

Industry observers note that if your mind tends to jump ahead to what your life would look like in a relationship, how it would feel to have a partner, and how this person fits into that picture, you may be more attached to the idea than the reality. As Moe Ari Brown, LMFT, therapist and Hinge’s in-house Love and Connection Expert explains, genuine interest feels grounded in the person themselves: “You should see them as a whole person, not a flattened version or a fantasy.” When you’re dating for validation, the emotional payoff often comes from imagining being chosen, rather than engaging with who the person sitting across from you actually is.

In a recent development, one of the more confusing dynamics is when everything feels strong while you’re together—conversation flows, there’s chemistry, maybe even a sense of closeness—but that energy doesn’t carry over once you leave. According to Sabrina Romanoff, PsyD, a clinical psychologist and relationship expert in Newly introduced York City, this can reflect “performative chemistry,” where the connection is heightened in the moment but not supported by real emotional investment. It can feel convincing because the highs are so high, but connection that only exists in person often signals that attention is the driving force.

Sources indicate that opening up is a key part of building intimacy, but when it happens too rapidly (read: love bombing and trauma dumping), it can function more as a shortcut than a foundation. Dr. Romanoff notes that oversharing early or rushing emotional and physical intimacy can create the illusion of connection without the substance of it. That early intensity can feel meaningful, but in many cases, it’s less about trust and more about accelerating closeness in a way that delivers immediate validation.

Industry observers note that you might text consistently, flirt easily, and maintain a steady stream of communication, but when it comes to actually making looks, things stay vague. “When someone is driven by their ego, they tend to keep people interested by dangling a carrot,” Dr. Romanoff notes, pointing to the way some people maintain attention without following through. You might keep the interaction alive because it feels good to be wanted without necessarily working to deepen the connection in a tangible way.

Interest that tends to spike at certain moments (i.e. late at night, when you’re bored, or when you’re craving attention) and then fades just as quickly can be revealing. Dr. Romanoff describes this pattern as fluctuating between “highs and lows,” where engagement is driven more by internal needs than sustained interest in the other person. When connection is the goal, effort tends to be steady; when validation is the goal, it often comes in waves.

If your conversations start to feel interchangeable with the same tone, same questions, and same level of interest across different people, your core goals may be less about building something specific and more about keeping options (and attention) open. Danielle Madonna, LCSW, a psychotherapist in Long Island, notes that this kind of behavior can reflect “a need for widespread validation rather than focused emotional investment.” Instead of getting to know one person more deeply, your focus stays on maintaining multiple streams of attention at once.

There’s a difference between excitement and pursuit. If you notice that your interest peaks when someone is slightly out of reach and then drops once they’re clearly available, it may be the chase (not the person) that’s keeping you engaged. “When enthusiasm diminishes after someone expresses real interest, it can signal that the primary drive may have been validation rather than intimacy,” states Madonna. “In other words, it’s not about connection—it’s about the feeling of being wanted.”.

In a recent development, according to Brown, the first step is removing any self-judgment once you acknowledge the pattern. “Wanting to feel affirmed in your dating choices is human,” he explains, and recognizing that can make it easier to shift your behavior without shame. From there, the work becomes more internal than external—getting clear on what you actually want a relationship to feel like rather than focusing on whether someone else chooses you. That might look like asking yourself simple but grounding questions: Do I feel at ease around this person? Am I curious about them? Do I feel like I can be myself, or am I performing? The more you anchor into your own experience, the less power external validation holds.

Recent findings suggest that it can also help to strip away the “audience” in your decision-making. Brown suggests imagining that no one else’s opinion matters (no social validation, no external approval), and then asking yourself whether you’d still be interested in the same people. Often, validation-driven dating shows up as choosing people who look good on paper but don’t feel good in practice. Shifting out of that cycle isn’t about forcing connection where it doesn’t exist—it’s about slowing down enough to notice what’s actually there. And when curiosity starts to replace performance—when you’re genuinely interested in who someone is and not just how they feel about you—that’s usually a sign you’re moving closer to real connection.

  • 1 The Rise, Stall, and Fall of Princes Gate• Concealing the Scar• Plans Without Progress • Fixing One Eyesore and Creating Another • The Breaking Point• Biting the Bullet • Back to Square One • Gone at Last?

Recent findings suggest that in 1979, the Victorian Government asked a deceptively simple question: What should Melbourne’s landmark be? The Melbourne Landmark Ideas Competition invited anyone—architects, artists, engineers, dreamers, and amateurs—to imagine a new symbol for the city on the neglected Jolimont rail yards opposite Flinders Street Station. The response was overwhelming: 2,300 proposals from around the world. They ranged from a giant Peach Melba and a building-sized chair to floating landmarks, megastructures, theme parks, monumental bridges, crystal pyramids, aquariums, laser beacons, and towers designed to rival the world’s great icons. One scheme proposed a gigantic clock spanning the Jolimont rail yards. Another imagined a crocodile large enough to swallow the Melbourne Cricket Ground. Unable to agree on a single scheme, the judges famously named forty-eight winners instead. Nothing was built.Nearly half a century later, architectural historian Derham Groves revisits this extraordinary episode in Melbourne’s history. Drawing on the original competition entries preserved in the Public Record Office Victoria, he reconstructs a moment when the city briefly opened itself to the world. Part detective story, cultural history, and cabinet of architectural curiosities, The 1979 Melbourne Landmark Ideas Competition: Lost Visions of a City’s Future uncovers the forgotten schemes, the people behind them, and the debates they provoked. The result is a vivid portrait of Melbourne at a turning point—when modernist certainty was fading, postmodern playfulness was emerging, and the future of the city seemed up for grabs. The competition never produced a landmark, but it left behind something more revealing: a dazzling record of how Melbourne once imagined its future—and how different that future might have been.

Magnus Ditlev Tells Us How He Traded Calamity in Kona for Glory in Florida

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance.
  • How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.
  • Industry observers note that thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a latest fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Magnus Ditlev finishes 2026 Ironman Florida in the fastest time at the full distance. (Photo: Ironman).

How we reported this: Triathlete contributor Travis Mundell interviewed Magnus Ditlev following the Dane’s fastest Ironman time of 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida to hear about what his training looked like after a DNF in Kona one month prior.

Industry observers note that thirty years after Lothar Leder became the first person to go under the eight-hour barrier at the full distance, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) set a latest fastest-ever time of seven hours and 19 minutes at Ironman Florida. Ditlev’s performance is even more impressive given it came just one month after imploding and pulling out roughly 30 minutes from a likely Ironman World Championship victory. But does it feel like retribution for the 29-year-old?

“What happened in Kona is still very much in my mind, and I’m probably thinking more about what happened in Kona right now than the world record, to be honest, because that was my substantial shot at a world championship title there, and being so close was very heartbreaking,” he told Triathlete, just days after his headline-grabbing race in Florida.

After finishing second at the Hawaii Ironman World Championship in 2024 and then winning Ironman South Africa in early 2025, Ditlev struggled to consistently reach the level that those performances suggest. And when a bout of shingles early in 2026 left him on the sidelines ahead of Ironman Texas, it seemed as if another season was in jeopardy.

Recent findings suggest that “I wasn’t in a good space because of all the sickness, and I think that was maybe still in the body somehow. Even though I was training OK, I wasn’t performing at races. And when I had to really push, I wasn’t able to do so,” Ditlev said, of his 11th-place finish at Ironman Frankfurt, where he narrowly secured a Kona qualifying slot. A sixth-place finish at Roth immediately followed, in a race where Sam Laidlow stopped the clock at a world’s best time of 7:21:04.

“That was hard to watch, especially because I was in the race, and I got absolutely humiliated in the race that has given me the most throughout my career, so that was really tough.”.

(Now that Ditlev has the record once more, Laidlow has since teased on Instagram that he is back in training to reclaim it).

Still, seeing the level of the competition gave Ditlev something to take away from the experience.

In a recent development, “Being in that race and seeing the level of Sam and the level of Kristian, it was good to get that kick in the butt,” he said. “That gave me that last little bit of motivation and push to try to get better.”.

Despite that added motivation, returning to the standards Ditlev had set for himself didn’t come without uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that “There were doubts every day, to be honest. I was doubting basically every step I took along the road, but I didn’t, or very rarely did I, change the intends because of those doubts.”.

That ability to stay the course is something he looks back on with pride.

According to recent reports, “That’s one of the things I’m proud of the most – that I never really veered off too much from that blueprint. I just tried to really work hard and do my best.”.

According to recent reports, sticking to the proposal slowly began to pay off behind the scenes: Ditlev headed to altitude in Nederland, Colorado, as he had before Kona in 2024 for his final training block. Finally, he saw some of the best training numbers of his career appearing across the swim, bike, and run.

“It was so simple where we were staying. It was just me, my girlfriend, and a coach some of the time, and we were just really focused on all the small things and living a simple life,” he explained. “I think going a bit away and not having too much to focus on apart from training and really trying to prepare for a good performance was definitely the thing I needed at that time.”.

Industry observers note that and for most of the race in Kona, those training numbers translated into exactly the performance he had hoped for. Ditlev led off the bike and maintained a commanding lead of more than four minutes throughout the run before his race unraveled under the heat and humidity in the final miles. Seemingly out of nowhere, he found himself seated on a barrier on the Queen K, having come so close to achieving his biggest goal.

According to recent reports, physically turning things around to race another Ironman in Florida in four weeks’ time was one type of challenge; mentally overcoming such a blow was another. Instead of returning home to Denmark, he flew back to Boulder, Colorado, to recover and restart training.

According to recent reports, “To be honest, it was quite tough. I had some days where I was really struggling to get out of the door because I was not really motivated and really had to push myself just to get out on the bike and ride,” he shared.

He acknowledged that it took more than his own resolve to get back out training.

“It was just the people around me that were so supportive, and they were trying to tell me that: ‘Yeah, look, you’re in amazing shape. If you manage to put yourself up to it mentally, then we think you can do amazing in Florida.”’.

At the same time, there was a physical concern in the back of everyone’s mind: whether the effects of the heat stress would linger — knowing Ditlev had gone deep into the well and far into the notoriously brutal 140-mile race.

“You hear those horror stories of people that have had heat injuries; they are out for long periods, and it could really sit in the system for a long time. So we were quite careful the first couple of days with the training to make sure that I was recovered, and then just didn’t do too much training in between [Kona and Florida].”.

Ditlev moved toward Florida with a lower total training volume, keeping a few bigger, specific sessions while focusing mainly on arriving fresh.

In a recent development, it worked, and the shape was still there. However, that freshness didn’t translate into race-day excitement. Instead, he was focused on qualifying for Kona and earning another chance to put things right.

Sources indicate that “I wasn’t too hyped up on the race as I’ve been before Kona, where I’m really looking forward to it so much. Whereas here I was just really relaxed. I think I knew I was in great shape and I wanted to execute, but I was not stressed or nervous that sometimes you can be before big races.”.

Sources indicate that the day began perfectly for Ditlev. One of the best swims of his career even saw him briefly take the lead after the Australian exit heading into the second lap.

It has been revealed that “When you have that swim, for me, then I know it’s gonna be a good day. It felt super easy and relaxed.”.

That set the tone for the rest of the race.

“I just felt like I was not working really hard the whole day, and that was the same for the bike and run. I was just doing my own race in control.”.

According to recent reports, that feeling of “not working really hard” produced the fastest bike split in Ironman history, averaging 29.3 mph — a number age groupers can’t even comprehend for an Olympic-distance race, let alone a full Ironman. To almost any age-group athlete, flying through the course in peak shape would sound like pure bliss. For Ditlev, it brought another sensation.

According to recent reports, “It was quite boring, to be honest, because it was a one-loop course and I didn’t see anyone at all. There was not even a motorbike or anything because the race wasn’t broadcast. So it was super lonely out there. I just tried to make time go by.”.

Industry observers note that thankfully for him, time went by quickly whether he felt it or not. Averaging 345 watts without dropping off power toward the end, he arrived in T2 with a 3:51:16 bike split and an 11-minute gap over the American chasers, including Sam Long, Rudy von Berg, and Ben Kanute.

After that swim and bike, Ditlev knew the fastest Ironman time was within reach. Before starting the run, he asked his girlfriend what marathon time he needed to secure it.

“I thought, ‘I can definitely do that, given how I’m feeling.’”.

Sources indicate that recounting the moment, Ditlev laughed as he described briefly debating whether to chase the record or take it easy with such an immense lead. Once again, the prospect of it being “too boring” helped him decide to “at least make the effort.”.

Starting at 3:35 per kilometer, or 5:46 per mile, he described the run as feeling “really smooth” until the final 8K, when he had to slow slightly. In the end, he still finished with a career-best 2:33:31 marathon. Despite that, and a fresh world’s best time, the specter of the Significant Island tempered his elation.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s probably because of Kona, but I wasn’t too hyped or too excited because it’s also in the back of my mind. This is what should have happened in Hawaii. So it’s a bit of a weird feeling.”.

It has been revealed that one of the biggest headline pieces of gear Ditlev debuted in Kona was his new, full-face-covering visor, which returned in Florida. Beyond its appearance, some questioned its practicality, wondering whether it would make the heat harder to manage. Ditlev swiftly dismissed that concern, saying, “It doesn’t make a big difference in how hot I feel.”.

But it wasn’t the visor that stole the attention in Florida; the biggest question about his setup was the lump in the center of his chest, with many speculating that it was some sort of latest cooling strategy.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s not for cooling. It’s just been a long time since I did a smaller Ironman race, and I found out there are no personal needs or pro fluids like there are in Kona, Roth, and Frankfurt that I’ve done this year.”.

The explanation was more practical than it looked.

“So I was having a hard time figuring out how I should carry my nutrition around the course. So actually, it’s just two 500 milliliter bottles with all my nutrition for the run.”.

After seeing the footage, however, he acknowledged the unusual appearance.

“It feels pretty natural, even though when I saw the videos, I can obviously see that it looks quite stupid.”.

When you’re aiming for 200 grams of carbohydrate per hour on the bike, and 150-160 grams on the run, carrying the nutrition took priority over appearances. But these insane grams-per-hour levels weren’t even the highest intake his team tested.

Recent findings suggest that “We did some tests with 220 actually, and it’s not the ceiling. It’s just becoming a diminishing return, if you can say it that way,” he explained. “I could probably add some more, but we are starting to go into really small potential benefits, and the consequences of it going wrong, or the risks, start to outweigh the potential rewards.”.

A performance like this makes it easy to imagine Ditlev as a childhood triathlon prodigy. Yet just 10 years ago, he was competing in his first age-group triathlon, with his only athletic background in football and badminton. Asked what he would tell that younger, 19-year-old Magnus, he laughed.

“Age-group Magnus didn’t even know that there was actually something called professional Ironman racing,” he said, before continuing, “Make sure that you are enjoying what you’re doing. If I didn’t enjoy it, I wouldn’t be doing it now. So just try to surround yourself with people that give you energy and stay curious about the process.”.

His latest time also raises an inevitable question: How much faster can he go?

First, Ditlev promptly kept the story straight: “It’s fun to set a fast time, but we are racing for wins,” before entertaining the thought experiment.

Recent findings suggest that “I don’t know if Florida is the fastest course in the world. It’s definitely a fast course. But some years it has been a wetsuit; then you are at least two minutes, maybe even three minutes quicker. Then, if you apply the transition zone that they have in Roth, which is something like four or five minutes quicker combined T2 time and T1, then we are somewhere between seven and eight minutes just from that.”.

The bike offered another potential saving.

“My bike engineer actually had me at 3:48 bike split before the race, but the wind conditions weren’t ideal on race day. So if you take a day with no wind, then I would probably be around 3:48, which is another three minutes. So then we are at about 10 minutes.”.

On the run, he had a wry smile as he pointed to third-place finisher Matt Hanson’s 2:28 marathon, not suggesting he could go that fast; he believed he could still squeeze out “a little bit more.”.

“I mean, probably 10 minutes, quite easily, quicker.”.

According to recent reports, for now, Ditlev is finally spending some time at home in Denmark after an extended stretch away. Not everyone embraces the off-season quite so readily – we’re looking at you, Taylor Knibb – but Ditlev says he is known among those close to him for being able to switch from some of the biggest training hours in the sport to almost none in a short space of time.

Amid the downtime, the fire still burns for a Kona title, with middle-distance and Ironman Pro Series racing taking a back seat to his preference for building toward specific goals.

Asked whether he wishes he could have a rematch against the now-retired Kona champion Vincent Luis, his answer was clear.

According to recent reports, “Of course. You want to beat the best people, and Vince was the best athlete in Kona that day. And I have to admit, when I saw that Vince was the guy that passed me first after I almost collapsed, I thought, ‘Okay, that’s actually pretty cool if he goes ahead and wins this race.’”.

Having spent time with Luis at altitude earlier in the year, Ditlev was happy to see him take the title off into retirement, even if it means missing the chance to race him again.

“He’s a really, really good guy, so I was super happy for him. And I thought it’s gonna be absolutely epic if he manages to keep it to the line. But yeah, of course, I’m sad that he’s retiring. It would be nice to race him next year as well.”.

Industry observers note that therefore, it’s best to pair GLP-1 agonists with modifications to your diet and lifestyle. A healthcare professional, such as a doctor or registered dietitian, can also provide ongoing guidance and support to promote long-term weight loss.

GLP-1 agonists are currently approved for three conditions: type 2 diabetes, obesity, and heart disease.

Keep in mind that these medications should be used alongside other lifestyle modifications, including changes to your diet and regular physical activity.

A doctor or other trusted healthcare professional can help determine whether a GLP-1 agonist may be beneficial for you, depending on your health concerns and goals.

Though GLP-1 agonists may support weight loss and help manage blood sugar levels, it’s notable to be aware of the possible side effects, such as vomiting, stomach pain, fatigue, constipation or diarrhea, mood changes, and more.

Because of the risk of side effects, it’s crucial to check in regularly with a healthcare professional. Additionally, it’s important to discuss any concerns you have about potential side effects with your doctor or other healthcare professional to make sure the medication is right for you.

Sources indicate that when you lose a lot of weight promptly, your body loses fat, but it also loses lean mass, including muscle and bone density. This is problematic because muscle is the “engine” of your metabolism, helping you burn energy even when you are resting.

Research reveals that people taking GLP-1 medications can lose a significant amount of muscle alongside fat. For example, in studies, about 15% to 40% of the total weight lost was lean mass. Exercise, such as strength training, can help preserve and build muscle while the medication helps you lose fat.

Sources indicate that exercise is also vital for bone health. Rapid weight loss is often linked to a reduction in bone mineral density, which can make bones weaker and more prone to fractures later in life.

According to recent reports, A 2024 analysis of a randomized clinical trial found that people using the GLP-1 liraglutide without exercising lost weight but had decreased bone density in the hips and spine. People who combined liraglutide with regular exercise experienced the best weight loss and preserved their bone mineral density.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that there’s no shortage of hacks, snacks, and habits that purportedly help you stay healthier for longer.
  • According to recent reports, one such staple is the humble roll of floss, which is probably collecting dust in your medicine cabinet.
  • Keep reading to see why skipping that single strand of string could have consequences that go far beyond tender gums.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that there’s no shortage of hacks, snacks, and habits that purportedly help you stay healthier for longer. But while we’re busy chasing cutting-edge upgrades—from cold plunges and greens powders to living by the gospel of your Oura ring—we tend to miss out on less sexy yet still powerful tweaks that have been shown to meaningfully move the needle on long-term health.

According to recent reports, one such staple is the humble roll of floss, which is probably collecting dust in your medicine cabinet. However, you should probably break it out nightly not just for a brighter, cleaner smile, but to potentially benefit your heart and brain, too.

Keep reading to see why skipping that single strand of string could have consequences that go far beyond tender gums.

In a recent development, if you believe that brushing twice daily will suffice for oral health, you’re in for some sobering news. According to Kami Hoss, DDS, author of If Your Mouth Could Talk: An In-Depth Guide to Oral Health and Its Impact on Your Entire Life, your toothbrush cleans only 60 percent of the surface of your teeth. Read: If you don’t floss, nearly half of your mouth goes uncleaned day after day.

Sources indicate that “Flossing is a simple but critical intervention because it disrupts bacterial biofilm between the teeth—areas a toothbrush cannot reach,” adds board-certified periodontist Richard Nejat, DDS. When you floss consistently, you reduce bacterial load, plaque buildup, and gum inflammation—all of which can help keep periodontal disease (a.k.a. gum disease) at bay. And there’s a decent chance you’ll be affected: Per the Cleveland Clinic, about half of adults in the U.S. have some form of gum disease.

The tissue surrounding these small crevices also warrants your full attention. “The sulcus—the shallow groove where your gum meets your tooth—is lined with some of the most permeable tissue in the human body,” Dr. Hoss tells SELF. “It’s richly vascularized, meaning bacteria and whatever compounds we introduce there have a remarkably direct pathway into the bloodstream.” And here’s where the longevity benefits of flossing come into play.

On top of staving off periodontal disease, research shows that regular flossing is associated with reduced risk of dementia, Alzheimer’s disease, and stroke. It can also be an vital part of managing diabetes. Meanwhile, poor flossing habits have been associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and CVD mortality. And according to one study of over 5,000 older adults, never flossing increased mortality risk by 30% compared to flossing daily.

In a recent development, so how can one tiny string make such a substantial difference in long-term health outcomes? For starters, you have some unfriendly bacteria to contend with. “Porphyromonas gingivalis, which occurs in the mouth, infects the gums and causes gum disease and periodontitis,” notes Jennifer Timmons, MD, a longevity physician and the founder of Timmons Wellness. She says that this bacteria is present in atherosclerotic plaque that can plug arteries during a heart attack, while Dr. Hoss adds that it’s also been found in the brain tissue of Alzheimer’s patients. That’s why addressing it at the source matters. “If you don’t floss, [the bacteria] can enter the bloodstream and lead to blood vessel inflammation, damage, and tiny blood clots that could cause heart attacks or strokes in other areas,” Dr. Timmons warns. (She notes that these are correlations, not proven causations, though the associations are strong.).

It has been revealed that flossing also actively helps decrease inflammation in the gums, thereby preventing a cascade of vascular damage throughout the body, Dr. Timmons explains. After all, inflammation is a major driver of not only gum disease but also the chronic conditions listed above. When you don’t floss, inflammation proliferates in the mouth—and it doesn’t stay put. “Chronic gum disease creates a systemic inflammatory burden that touches almost every major disease category,” Dr. Hoss warns. That doesn’t mean flossing is a panacea, but it highlights how interconnected oral health and overall health really are.

If you already floss daily, rest assured that you’re ahead of the game. For the rest of us who skimp here and there—or have yet to make flossing routine, despite the awkward biannual urges from our dentist—now’s a great time to pick up the habit.

Dr. Hoss advises flossing at night rather than in the morning. “You’re sealing your mouth for six to eight hours. Clearing that biofilm before bed matters far more than doing it after breakfast,” he says. He also recommends good old string floss above the likes of picks and water flossers, as neither can get into the nooks and crannies at and below the gumline as efficiently. (If traditional floss is tough to maneuver, these alternatives are still better than skipping it altogether.) As for the right way to floss? “Curve it into a ‘C’ shape around each tooth and use an up-and-down motion,” he shares.

It has been revealed that in short, flossing is crucial to maintain oral health, and good oral health has clear downstream effects on the rest of the body. Since heart disease remains the leading cause of death in the United States—and dementia significantly impacts both quality and length of life —anything that meaningfully reduces risk, even modestly, matters in the longevity conversation. “While flossing alone is not a cure-all for heart or brain health, it is one of the easiest daily habits that can support both oral and overall health,” says Dr. Nejat. All remarked, flossing might not be revolutionary, but it has surprisingly far-reaching potential.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • So often we have our dream destinations on reserve for the day we can go with the person we’ve agreed to spend our life with.
  • Industry observers note that for my most recent we-moon, I was invited to the Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla and joined by two girlfriends.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that I’m on a speedboat whizzing towards my latest vacation destination. As we bounce along, I attempt to take a selfie. The shot I want is the waves, the boats, the islands, but I can’t seem to get the kissing couples out the background. No matter which way I turn, there are honeymooners in my viewfinder. The boat operators and I are the only single people on this vessel. Technically I, too, am a part of a couple—actually, a throuple of single girlfriends heading for an Anguilla getaway. The trip is what I like to call a we-moon.

So often we have our dream destinations on reserve for the day we can go with the person we’ve agreed to spend our life with. There’s the honeymoon and the babymoon, but when do single women get to celebrate life milestones and fulfill the desire for companionship and adventure? That’s the we-moon.

Industry observers note that for my most recent we-moon, I was invited to the Four Seasons Resort and Residences Anguilla and joined by two girlfriends. Now, you are probably wondering: What is the difference between this and your average girls trip? Well, similar to a honeymoon or babymoon, a we-moon is taken to celebrate a major life milestone. For me, it was my first book. Single women are so often traveling to celebrate others for their bachelorette or wedding or baby shower. Rarely do we get friends to travel and celebrate something that doesn’t fit into the typical timeline.

In a recent development, that is the purpose of a we-moon. It’s making the phone call to ask your friends to travel and celebrate an achievement with you, just like you do for others. It could be a promotion, a new job, a masters degree, or a book deal.

When crafting the perfect we-moon, there are things to keep in mind to make sure that the trip goes smoothly. I spoke to Joy Harden Bradford, PhD, author of Sisterhood Heals about the best way to pull off a destination celebration with no drama.

Industry observers note that on a honeymoon or babymoon, the whole point is to spend more time together. On a we-moon, it’s a balance of time together and time alone. That’s why Dr. Bradford recommends separate rooms if your budget allows. For this Anguilla trip, we were staying in a villa rental, so we all had our own room and bathroom. It was perfect for the early risers who wanted to read a book on their balcony quietly, or late sleepers who wanted to lay in and order room service. This location was perfect for the we-moon because the Four Seasons Villa and Residence Rentals have the privacy of a personal home but you still can tap into hotel amenities and personalized services (more on that below). Whatever you decide, you should talk about it ahead of time.

“I think having a place where everybody can retreat and have alone time is really good if that is something that the group can do. So private sleeping quarters are important,” she notes. “Also having conversations about budget ahead of time. Because some people [might say], ‘Oh, we don't need a five-star hotel. We’re just going to be there to sleep. We’re going to be out.’ And other people are like, ‘No, I like luxury.’ So you don’t want to wait until you get there to find out that there’s a difference in the group about that.”.

It has been revealed that another thing you should talk about ahead of time is how many group excursions everyone is down to do. “Because I think for a lot of us, there’s so much going on in our regular life that there’s a lot of expectations for what a vacation should be,” notes Dr. Bradford. “‘It’s the one time I get to get away,’ and so people really put a lot on it.”.

Sources indicate that there are many different vacation styles. We’ve all been on a trip that is overplanned and leaves you more exhausted than when you left. Everyone should discuss what activities they want to do, and a good portion should be optional. For example, we worked on an itinerary with our villa concierge. When it came time to do the private yoga session poolside, some people wanted to rest. So I locked in for a one-on-one session, in which I was able to pay extra attention to modifications and my personal pain points. There were plenty of things that we did together, like an afternoon at the spa, where we all got Anguilla-themed massages, and an excursion across the island in a Jeep to see a different beach. Sometimes you just want to take a nap on vacation, and that is okay.

Me doing yoga with my instructor by the villa pool.

Industry observers note that one of the things we did as a group was a margarita-making class. The three of us lined up at the bar of the villa and learned how to properly shake and measure lime juice, orange liqueur, and tequila. Research says that picking up a fresh skill is good for your brain health. (Although I’m not sure they meant consuming three margaritas in an hour….) The new experience for you can be learning a new sport like pickleball, going to a cooking class, or even playing board games by the beach. This is even better when it becomes a social experiment because even if you fail, you can laugh it off with friends.

Industry observers note that what is a girls trip without girl talk? You have to set the mood for conversations. It’s not always a good time to dive deep into your last breakup as you are sitting at a noisy restaurant or relaxing at a spa appointment. But when you are away from your regular routine, there is a great opportunity to open up. “If these are people that you’re actually hoping to grow closer to, then it is notable to continue to go deeper with those relationships. And that really requires a lot of vulnerability, which is really hard for people,” says Bradford. “Girls trips really provide a great opportunity and a great backdrop because you are away from your regular routine to maybe get into some of those things that you don’t have time to talk about later.” You have to set the mood for your friends to unravel. For me, I planned a night in the villa's private jacuzzi tub, watching the sunset, and drinking wine. That’s where we shared our work woes and dating troubles as a night cap.

My friends and I having girl talk by the fire.

#182939. 13 Black Women Share How They Found the Strength to Survive—and Thrive—With Breast Cancer

📅 18 Oct 2021 • ⏱️ 22m • 📚 Deep Dive (4463 w)
