💡 Key Takeaways
  • Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • It has been revealed that bicycle helmets have saved my life more times than I can count.
  • While some lids from decades past were bulky and sometimes looked silly, modern road, mountain, and commuter helmets combine safety, performance, and style.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

It has been revealed that bicycle helmets have saved my life more times than I can count. I’ve ridden and raced bikes for most of my life, so unfortunately I’ve hit the deck many times on trails and on roads. That’s why I wear a helmet anytime I kit up, clip in, and head out for a ride.

While some lids from decades past were bulky and sometimes looked silly, modern road, mountain, and commuter helmets combine safety, performance, and style. While a helmet’s primary role is to protect your head and brain in a crash, the best bike helmets also look great, and some even improve your speed.

Helmet technology has improved considerably in the last decade. Plus, safety features once limited to high-end helmets have trickled down to affordable models. Rider safety has also improved: independent testing by Virginia Tech has prompted more manufacturers to incorporate anti-rotational features across all helmet styles, categories, and price levels. Additionally, high-tech materials, improved ventilation, better straps, and more aerodynamic shapes make today’s lids lighter, cooler, and faster than those from only a few years ago.

Picking the perfect helmet can be challenging. Brands offer scores of models in every possible riding category. Whether you ride on asphalt, gravel roads, or dirt trails, you can find a helmet that matches your style, fit, and budget needs.

Expert Advice: Buy the helmet that feels the most comfortable on your head. You are more likely to use a helmet that fits and feels great, and that’s the first step in keeping your noggin safe if you crash.

Sources indicate that elite road and gravel helmets offer low weight, excellent ventilation, and great looks. However, those benefits usually come at a high cost. Giro’s Agilis Mips helmet is a great option if you want a pro-level look and performance without the associated price.

Weighing 299 grams (size medium), my Agilis is only 15 grams heavier than Giro’s premium Aries Spherical model—and the Agilis costs $230 less. The Agilis is very well-ventilated, comparable to the priciest lids on all but the hottest of rides.

Industry observers note that giro offers eight color options for the Agilis, so you’re sure to find one that matches your riding kits, bike, and personal style. This helmet features Mips technology to protect your brain from rotational forces in a crash, and Giro’s Hardbody co-molded shell to better protect it from small bumps and dings when not on your head. Plus, the Agilis is equipped with Roc-Loc dial system to ensure a proper fit.

It has been revealed that with a five-star rating and 8.14 STAR score, the P2R A20 Mips places third in Virginia Tech’s road helmet rankings (and eleventh overall). That ranking is great for any road or gravel helmet—but for a helmet that costs only $60, it’s downright amazing.

According to recent reports, P2R somehow hits the A20’s low price without cutting many corners on features. It has nice straps with adjustable quick clamps that offer plenty of adjustment. P2R also includes a USB-rechargeable light that magnetically clips into the rear vent for commuting or extra visibility on the road. The one downside we found with the A20 Mips is that it feels optimized for rounder head shapes. While it fits me well, a couple of others who tried it mentioned the A20 fits a little snug near their temples.

TOP 5 RANKED VA TECH ROAD HELMETS.

Recent findings suggest that although it costs less than $80, I reach for the Lazer Tonic KinetiCore as often as helmets triple its price. The Tonic looks good and fits great, and at only 247 grams, it’s lighter than many more expensive lids I own. Plus, it features 18 vents for good airflow on hot days. Another thing I like about the Tonic KinetiCore is the options: Lazer offers it in nine colors and four sizes. This means you’re almost guaranteed to find one that fits your head and personal style.

Sources indicate that overall, the Tonic KinetiCore looks, feels, and rides like much pricier helmets. It combines low weight, ventilation, and protection into an affordable package. The Tonic uses Lazer’s proprietary KinetiCore system; it reduces weight and integrates rotational impact protection. This is a solid lid for your daily road and gravel rides or even commutes.

Recent findings suggest that for the Aries Spherical, Giro improved ventilation and aerodynamics over its previous range-topping Aether model. It is an excellent, pro-level road lid for road riders seeking superior performance and fit. It’s lightweight, super-adjustable, and is offered in tons of colors—including Visma-Lease a Bike and Canyon-SRAM special editions.

Recent findings suggest that the Aries also has excellent safety features—I know how well the Aries Spherical works because I personally crash-tested it late last year. Giro incorporates its Spherical nested-shell (ball-in-socket) design for rotational-force protection in a crash and improved energy dissipation. The Aries also uses Giro’s Aura reinforcement bridges to keep the foam in place during impact. These features earned the Aries an excellent five-star rating from Virginia Tech. It ranks in the top fifteen overall and fifth in road helmets.

Sources indicate that the Smith Network Mips employs many features from the company’s pricier models, along with some truly novel ones. It retains the honeycomb-like Koroyd panels that absorb energy upon impact. The Network also features an optional fabric visor for the convenience of a cycling cap without the added bulk.

Sources indicate that since Smith (a sunglass organization) makes this helmet, it has great eyewear integration. Color options are another upside to the Network; there is one to match virtually any rider’s style.

Recent findings suggest that P2R’s A70 Pro is probably the best deal for a performance road helmet. At only $100, the A70 punches well above its price. It packs the fit, finish, and adjustability we expect from much pricier lids. Plus, this P2R helmet features a Mips liner and earned a four-star rating from Virginia Tech’s helmet lab.

It has been revealed that for the price, it’s an excellent helmet, but it has a few downsides. While it wasn’t noticeable while riding, the A70 Pro is a bit heavier than competitors’ pricier aero helmets. Fit-wise, the A70 fit our test riders’ medium-sized heads, but medium is the smallest size available. Lastly, we lost two pairs of glasses from the helmet’s sunglass port, so maybe don’t use that feature.

Aero helmets are a good way to save watts and boost your speed. That’s why you see so many pro racers choosing these sleek lids, even on the warmest days of Grand Tour events. Giro’s upcoming Eclipse Pro is one of the best choices available, and one of the year’s hottest pieces of cycling equipment.

In a recent development, weighing 280 grams (claimed), the Eclipse Pro is light for an aero helmet, and competes with some brands’ lightweight models. And thanks to improved aerodynamics, Giro claims the Pro is 17% faster than its predecessor, the Eclipse Spherical. Giro also packs the Eclipse Pro with safety features, including its Spherical (anti-rotational), Aura II (reinforcement), and Progressive Layering (dual-density EPS foam) technologies.

Riding POC’s Cytal Mips in 100-degree heat on Stage 5 of the 2026 Tour de France, I learned first-hand how well this helmet ventilates your head. Senior Photographer Trevor Raab backed up my findings in his test riding. He remarked, “On fast-paced hot rides, it offered a noticeable increase in cooling as well as remaining comfortable while slowly slogging up climbs.”.

Like other POC helmets, the Cytal combines Scandinavian style and excellent safety into one package. Although the Cytal’s fit runs large, it’s easy to dial in with its adjustable retention system and different padding options. Raab has an approximately 58cm head and falls between sizes (medium and large). Similarly, I consistently wear a size medium from other brands and found the medium was a little large on my head. If you can size down, it may offer a more streamlined and aero fit.

Expert Advice: Most riders know they should replace a helmet after they crash. But did you know that your helmet can expire? Helmets don’t have an actual best-by date, but the general rule of thumb is to replace your lid every three to five years. So, if you’re wondering, “When did I get this helmet?”, it might be time to replace it.

According to recent reports, TLD’s full-face helmets have been the go-to choice of top downhill, freeride, and enduro riders for decades. Since launching the A1 trail helmet more than ten years ago, Troy Lee Designs has led the mountain bike market in comfort, fit, and style. The A3 Mips, the brand’s top-tier trail helmet, takes what makes TLD lids legendary to a newly introduced level.

Recent findings suggest that senior Test Editor Matt Phillips has ridden the A3 for countless hours on the trails of Durango, Colorado, and gives it a ringing endorsement. He states, “The TLD A3, since its launch a couple of years ago, has risen to the top of my favorite MTB helmets list. The style and color options are a highlight, of course—it’s a TLD. But what makes this helmet a standout is its secure fit and comfort. It locks onto my head and doesn’t wiggle or bounce, yet produces no pressure points. I also appreciate the adjustable visor when the sun is low (or high), reasonably solid eyewear docking, and the super-effective sweat-diverting brow strip, which keeps glasses and goggles dry.”.

In a recent development, smith recently introduced the Pilot, and for only $95, it’s a great overall package. The Pilot features Mips protection, a fit dial, and lightweight straps. The helmet also has great compatibility with glasses and goggles (which only seems right considering eyewear brand Smith makes it). Senior Photographer Trevor Raab tested the Pilot and provided some ride notes.

“Helmets can get expensive, and there are lots of premium features driving the price up on MTB lids. The Pilot gives you everything you need and nothing you don’t without breaking the bank,” Raab remarked. He additionally notes that “the straps with adjusters that wouldn't seem out of place on helmets costing 2x the price.” The only drawback he has found is the Pilot’s fixed visor: “For those who like to fine-tune their peak, it’s a bit of a drag, but I’m not complaining at this price.”.

Industry observers note that the Schwinn Intercept is a $30 helmet and is ranked four stars in Virginia Tech’s STAR testing. That’s a higher ranking than several helmets that VA Tech tested, some of which cost hundreds of dollars more. Though it’s inexpensive, the Interceptor still features a dial-adjustable fit system and a removable visor. It’s a one-size-fits-most model with a claimed weight of about 350 grams—surprisingly light for an affordable helmet.

Sources indicate that finding a trail-style mountain bike helmet that looks good, has a 5-star rating from Virginia Tech, and is priced less than $100 is a tall order. However, Endura pulled it together with its Hummveee Mips model.

British-brand Endura is best-known for its excellent riding apparel, but its mountain bike helmets are also worth a look. The Hummvee features a Mips liner to protect against rotational forces in a crash, a removable visor, and in-mold construction to improve durability. While it’s a one-size-fits-most helmet, Endura offers this lid in three color choices: black, red, and white.

It has been revealed that if you’re commuting by e-bike, you’ll want to wear a helmet. However, not all commuter lids are rated for e-bike use. Unit 1’s Aura smart helmet not only passes NTA8776 and EN1078 safety standards, but it also earned a five-star rating from Virginia Tech’s helmet lab and ranks third among all commuter helmets.

According to recent reports, the Aura also has several built-in features to increase your visibility to drivers. These include 350-lumen head and taillights, turn signals, crash detection, and a Fidlock buckle. It even pairs with Bosch e-bikes.

Industry observers note that this tech comes at a price—in both dollars and grams. At $260, it’s not the cheapest commuter helmet, but it’s arguably the best equipped. The Aura’s 469-gram weight (measured, size medium) is noticeable while riding, and it can feel a little heavy the first few times you wear it.

Inspired by vintage motorcycle helmets, the Thousand Heritage is trendy and comfortable. Recently updated, the Heritage 2.0 retains its faux-leather strap and now features larger vents on the top and in the back to keep you cool. It also has a rear dial so you can adjust the fit for your head shape and hairstyle, and we had no trouble managing the helmet’s magnetic buckle with just one hand. The Heritage’s logo also hides a unique feature: It pops off to reveal a small channel through which you can run a lock to secure the helmet. This is handy if you don’t want to carry your lid around once you reach your destination.

In a recent development, our team thoroughly vetted each helmet on this list. Collectively, we log tens of thousands of miles each year wearing these helmets (and dozens more), in all kinds of conditions. Our test team rides on pavement and gravel, trail rides and bike park laps, daily commutes, and quick spins around town.

We evaluated each helmet based on performance, value, fit, comfort, ventilation, aerodynamics, adjustability, and looks. We also consider Virginia Tech safety ratings when available. The result is a selection of helmets that deliver the best experience across every budget and riding style.

According to recent reports, you probably already know where you like to ride. Perhaps you ride on paved roads, or maybe on gravel and dirt. Other cyclists prefer riding mountain bikes in the woods or on the rail trail with the family.

Industry observers note that helmets are generally grouped by cycling discipline—road, gravel, mountain, commuting, or recreational. But don’t feel boxed in by those labels—You can wear a mountain bike lid for gravel rides, commute in a lightweight road helmet, or don a commuter helmet for weekend rides on the bike path. The best helmet is the one that you will wear—something that fits well, feels good, and meets your budget.

However, it’s still helpful to understand what those category designations actually mean in terms of helmet features, ventilation, and protection:.

Recent findings suggest that you can spend as little as $30 for a helmet or more than $400 on a high-end race lid. Generally, pricier helmets are lighter and better ventilated. However, all helmets sold in the U.S. must meet the same CPSC safety standards.

For a deep dive into Virginia Tech’s independent helmet testing program, read Matt Phillip’s excellent story, “Virginia Tech’s Upcoming Helmet Ratings Raise the Bar. Here’s How the Tougher System Could Affect Your Next Choice.”.

All helmets sold in the U.S. must meet a Consumer Product Safety Commission (CPSC) standard. However, the standard was adopted in 1998. For example, it does not give specifics for mitigating rotational forces on the brain. It also does not lay down any standards for a full-face helmet’s chin bar.

In a recent development, voluntary and third-party tests go beyond the CPSC standard. We like Virginia Tech’s STAR tests, which were developed with a more modern understanding of head injuries than the CPSC’s test. VA Tech’s protocols evaluate a helmet’s ability to mitigate linear acceleration and rotational velocity, then assign a ranking of zero to five stars. A helmet receives more stars if Virginia Tech’s testing indicates it does a better job of reducing injury. VA Tech only recommends helmets that receive four or five stars.

Outside of CPSC and VA Tech’s STAR, most reputable helmet makers have their own in-house test protocols. The specifics of those tests and the results are often proprietary and not shared with the public.

According to recent reports, remember, no controlled test can replicate every possible real-world crash, but wearing a helmet is always better than not wearing one. Additionally, manufacturers’ understanding of what makes an effective helmet improves every day, which means helmets are always improving.

Sizes vary by brand, and most companies offer fit guides to help you choose the best size for your head. Measure your head’s circumference to determine the best size. If you fall between sizes, choose the most comfortable helmet.

Recent findings suggest that the correct size helmet will sit low and straight on your forehead. The retention system should take up some of the slack so the helmet sits securely on your head—you shouldn’t rely on cinching down the chin strap to hold the helmet in place. The right helmet will fit comfortably, and the retention system will easily snug up the fit.

Consider these other factors when choosing and purchasing a upcoming helmet.

Sources indicate that typically, road helmets are the lightest and best ventilated helmets. In some cases, the vents even also enhance cooling (over wearing no helmet at all) by directing airflow through carefully designed shapes and vents and over your head. This also helps prevent your sunglasses from fogging. Other helmets with increased coverage, such as full-face and mountain bike helmets, often have fewer vents.

Recent findings suggest that however, don’t get tricked into thinking that “more vents are better.” You can’t judge a helmet’s cooling ability only by its number of vents. The Giro Synthe, for example, has only 19 vents but is widely regarded as well-ventilated, while the Kask Valegro has a whopping 37 vents. The size and design of the vents, plus thoughtful internal channels, are more crucial than the quantity.

Weight needn’t be your biggest concern because when it comes to a helmet, the one you wear will always win out over the one you don’t. It comes down to comfort—you’re more likely to wear a helmet that won’t get in the way or weigh you down.

In a recent development, lightweight helmets tend to feel more comfortable, especially on long or challenging rides. Both material choices and design aspects contribute to weight savings. High-tech helmets often save grams by incorporating intricate internal bridges and supports that allow airflow and keep the helmet together in a crash. But be prepared to pay a higher price for these innovations. Opting out of “extras” like visors and mounts will also reduce weight.

While we don’t recommend adorning your helmet with too many accessories, extras such as visors, GoPro mounts, and lights certainly have their place and time.

Industry observers note that if you find yourself riding in the dark, light mounts can make your life easier and safer by illuminating the path ahead and providing a rear-facing blinker light to help drivers see you in low-light conditions. Bike commuters especially should consider light mounts to make the morning and evening transitions as smooth as possible. Helmet-mounted bike lights work great in conjunction with handlebar-mounted lights because they move with you when you turn your head.

Recent findings suggest that for those who ride during daylight, visors provide a built-in sun shield, especially for mountain bikers or rec riders. Road riders may use a cycling cap under the helmet and eschew any helmet-related extras.

Most modern helmets come equipped with safety technology such as Mips, KinetiCore, Koroyd, and WaveCel.

In a recent development, these technologies are engineered to help reduce the forces transmitted to your brain from impacts and collisions in different ways. However, no system or technology can guarantee a better outcome in every situation.

When researching a helmet’s protection, consider rotational and direct-impact forces. Choose a lid that uses a time-tested safety system. Look for positive reviews from actual owners, not only quotes from brands. Full-spectrum protection might cost more than the most bare-bones helmet, but it’s worth the price for frequent riders and anyone who ventures off the beaten path onto gnarly singletrack or into heavy traffic.

Recent findings suggest that mips (Multi-Directional Impact Protection System) is the most widely know helmet technology. It comes in several versions and is used by numerous helmet brands.The most common Mips tech uses a liner inside the helmet that allows your head and helmet to move relative to each other in the event of a crash. Upon impact, the helmet can move without pulling on your head, which claims to reduce brain trauma. Mips Spherical found on some Giro models is variant. The MIPS SL pads in the Specialized Prevail III is another example.

KinetiCore uses blocks and channels in the helmet’s EPS foam designed to create crumple zones that absorb energy under impact impact.Lazer claims KinetiCore improves ventilation, reduces weight, and limits plastic use in its helmets.

Koroyd uses miniature tubes thermo-welded to create a honeycomb shape. The material crumples in on itself upon impact. Smith typically applies Koroyd in a zonal manner, built into particular places on the helmet to optimize weight and space savings while protecting the most vulnerable parts of your head. Smith’s latest helmet models employ Koroyd and Mips for a double dose of leading-edge protection.

Industry observers note that used in four Trek helmet models, Wavecel is a 15mm-thick grid of layered polyester intended to crumple, flex, and glide on impact. Trek claims this system reduces forces on the rider’s head.

In addition to standard road, mountain, and commuter helmets, some brands offer full-face and e-bike-rated helmets.

Only the Netherlands has an e-bike-specific helmet standard (adopted there in 2017). NTA 8776 is a standard designed to protect against higher-impact speeds and covers a slightly larger part of the head.

Sources indicate that in the U.S., there are presently no helmet requirements specific to e-bike use. However, several manufacturers sell commuter helmets built to the NTA 8776 standard. Two of our favorites are the Specialized Mode and the Smith Dispatch MIPS.

Sources indicate that the helmets in this story are “half-shells” and cover the top of the head. Their coverage usually ends around the eyebrows and top of the ears, though some—particularly mountain bike helmets—extend to the back of the rider’s head.

Another style of helmet is the full face. As the name suggests, this style covers most of a rider’s head and has a chin bar to protect the rider’s jaw. A full-face helmet covers the ears and the back of the head, with a large opening in front that allows a rider to wear goggles.

Industry observers note that full-face helmets protect more of the rider’s head—particularly the mouth and jaw—but are heavier and less ventilated than traditional cycling helmets. Full face helmets are primarily used by mountain bikers—especially downhill and enduro racers—but all riders can benefit from the extra protection they provide.

Sources indicate that as Deputy Editor, Tara Seplavy leads Bicycling’s product test team; after having previously led product development and sourcing for multiple bike brands, run World Championship winning mountain bike teams, wrenched at renowned bicycle shops in Brooklyn, raced everything from criteriums to downhill, and ridden bikes on six different continents (landing herself in hospital emergency rooms in four countries and counting). Based in Easton, Pennsylvania, Tara spends tons of time on the road and trail testing products. A familiar face at cyclocross races, crits, and bike parks in the Mid Atlantic and New England, on weekends she can often be found racing for the New York City-based CRCA/KruisCX team. When not riding a bike, or talking about them, Tara listens to a lot of ska, punk, and emo music, and consumes too much social media.

Breaking: The Best Elliptical Machines for a Low-Impact Cardio Workout at Home

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Elliptical machines have come a long way, with major developments in specs and technology.
  • Sources indicate that if you are on the hunt for the best elliptical of 2025 but aren’t sure where to start, you’ve come to the right place.
  • In a recent development, the NordicTrack FS10i isn’t your average elliptical—it combines a treadmill, elliptical, and stair stepper all into one machine designed to give you the flexibility to switch up your cardio.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Elliptical machines have come a long way, with major developments in specs and technology. Their ergonomic design maximizes the quality and intensity of your workout, incorporating both upper and lower body muscles. This provides you with a full-body workout to enhance your cardio fitness while maintaining the structural integrity of your joints. We consider that an all-around win.

Sources indicate that if you are on the hunt for the best elliptical of 2025 but aren’t sure where to start, you’ve come to the right place. Below, you’ll find our top picks for the best elliptical machines and a comprehensive guide on what to consider before you make your purchase.

In a recent development, the NordicTrack FS10i isn’t your average elliptical—it combines a treadmill, elliptical, and stair stepper all into one machine designed to give you the flexibility to switch up your cardio. The 32-inch adjustable stride adjusts based on your leg movements. In other words, if you use the FS10i as a stair stepper, your legs move up and down, but your stride goes back and forth in elliptical mode.

It has been revealed that you can follow an iFIT class (with a $39/month subscription) on the 10-inch HD touchscreen, which tracks key stats such as time elapsed, speed, distance, and calories burned. Trainers can digitally adjust your incline up to 10 percent or tap into the 24 resistance levels based on the workout. If you’re working out manually, you can make these adjustments yourself via one-touch buttons next to the touchscreen.

If you’re on a fitness journey, a weight-loss diet and exercise are essential to achieving your goals. If you already have a favorite weight-loss program or weight-loss app, an elliptical can help you knock out your daily sweat session. While any elliptical will help you work toward your goal, the E95 stands out thanks to its free fitness app and integrated streaming services, perfect for when you need more motivation to get moving. Unlike some of the other ellipticals on our list, the E95’s companion app, Sole+, is free with your fresh machine. Sole+ includes more than 3,000 trainer-led workouts and classes for on and off your elliptical. For even more entertainment while you work out, the E95 is integrated with several streaming services, including Netflix, Amazon Prime, Hulu, and more.

The Sole E95’s cushioned foot pedals are designed to keep your knees and ankles from feeling the brunt of an extended workout. The pedals adjust to fit your gait, but default to a two-degree inward angle. The Sole E95’s 20 resistance levels let you challenge yourself and can be easily switched via buttons on the handles. Sole’s drive system is engineered to stay quiet, but if you want to listen to your class or music on its built-in speakers, simply plug in your smart device and prop it up in the inserted tablet holder.

RELATED: Best Home Gym Equipment.

Industry observers note that the Sole E35 Elliptical is a great choice for anyone looking for a reliable, simple elliptical with a smooth ride for joint comfort. It’s easy to set up and use and has everything you need to start working out in the comfort of your own home—no gym membership required.

The Sole E35’s ramp-like design allows customers to simply step on and start moving. With this elliptical, you can get a full-body workout without having to worry about straining your back or joints. It is equipped with 20 different levels of resistance so users can adjust their workouts according to their fitness levels and goals. With 10 preloaded workout programs plus free access to the Sole+ fitness app, even beginners can start their training immediately. Even though it’s not as heavy-duty as other ellipticals, the  Sole E35 works for users up to 300 pounds.

And while it comes with all the features you’d expect from an elliptical, it also has some great extras that we love: built-in fans keep you cool during workouts, and a user-friendly, fully adjustable console ensures a comfortable workout.

RELATED: Best Budget Home Gym Equipment.

If you’re short on space but looking to up your cardio workout with an elliptical, take a look at the Bowflex Max Trainer M6. Bringing together form and function, the M6 stamps out a footprint measuring just 46 inches long, 26 inches wide, and 64.2 inches high—quite a bit smaller than your average treadmill or other cardio machine. Its 15-inch stride length may not be a great fit for taller individuals, but it still supports a user weight of up to 300 pounds.

It has been revealed that the M6 offers a great workout with 16 levels of resistance, a USB charging port, a water bottle holder, Bluetooth heart rate compatibility, and multi-grip moving handles with pulse contact grips to measure heart rate. It’s also equipped with a unique burn rate display to track how many calories you burn per minute and allows you to set activity level targets throughout the workout.

Recent findings suggest that if interactive programming is your jam, you’re in luck. The JRNY digital fitness platform for Bowflex products houses tailored workouts, on-demand classes, real-time coaching, and personalized programming. Purchasing the M6 gives you a free membership to JRNY. Download the workout app, place your device in the magnetic media, and get pedaling.

In a recent development, bowflex offers in-home assembly for an additional fee, which we recommend because assembly takes a few hours (according to reviewers). The warranty is a bit disappointing, offering only two years on the frame and parts. Most competitors cover the frame with a 10-year warranty, so you’ll want to make sure your Bowflex is assembled correctly.

In a recent development, the little elliptical that could, the Cubii Go provides an elliptical experience for a fraction of the space and price. This portable elliptical fits seamlessly underneath your desk and can be taken on the go with its built-in wheels and retractable handle.

Industry observers note that unlike under-desk treadmills, you don’t have to stand to work out with the Cubii Go. Instead, you can stay seated and pedal during a meeting or while watching TV. Its large flywheel lets you go up to ten resistance levels while an illuminated display projects your stats back to you. Use the Cubii app to keep track of the details of your workout plus. The Cubii Go is also easy to take with you, thanks to built-in wheels and a double telescoping handle.

In a recent development, this compact elliptical presently has an average rating of 4.8 out of 5 stars on the Cubii website. Out of 238 reviews, only five give the Cubii Go one star. Negative ratings include criticism of the machine’s stability and design. Four-star reviews praise the Cubii Go as effective and easy to use.

In a recent development, if you’re a first-time elliptical buyer who’s feeling a little intimidated by the whole process, you might find the Niceday Smart Elliptical CT11 a comfortable option. Equipped with large pedals and constructed with steel, the Niceday Elliptical trainer can support users up to 400 pounds. It’s also designed to fit users between 4’9″ and 6’4″ tall, although it’s worth noting that the 15.5-inch stride length may feel restrictive to people on the taller end of that range. This elliptical also comes 90 percent pre-assembled, a feature sure to appeal to those less mechanically inclined. If you find quiet workouts comfortable, you’ll appreciate the Smart Elliptical CT11’s magnetic drive system. It’s designed to reduce noise and keep the sound of the machine below 20 decibels—about the same amount of noise as rustling leaves.

This elliptical trainer offers 16 levels of resistance, so you can use it for anything from light workouts to more intense leg and glute exercises. It’s also compatible with Kinomap and digitally records stats including speed, distance, calories, and heart rate.

The Niceday Smart Elliptical CT11 has an average rating of 4.4 out of 5 stars on Amazon with nearly 3,000 reviews. While most Amazon feedback is complimentary about the machine’s performance, criticisms include noise level and suitability for taller users.

Recent findings suggest that elliptical machines are an excellent choice for people looking for a low-impact, total-body cardio workout of any intensity. “You’re using both your arms and your legs to propel yourself, and you can adjust the resistance based on what works for you,” claims Samantha April, P.T., D.P.T., U.S.A.-W. They’re also great for people with balance problems. “Someone may use an elliptical over a treadmill if they’re looking for something that’s a little more controlled and they want to move with the machine and keep their feet stationary versus a treadmill where they’re required to move,” says April.

Industry observers note that however, elliptical machines are not ideal for people with small home gym spaces. “If space is a concern inside of your home gym, ellipticals take up a pretty fair amount of space, so it’s crucial that you’ll actually have the space to accommodate that,” April states.

People can do a variety of workouts on an elliptical trainer, from slow, easy walks to fast and intense interval sessions.

Sources indicate that don’t forget to warm up with some deep breaths and stretching. When you’re ready, place your feet on the pedals and grab the handles. Begin moving your feet forward in a general walking motion.

Although you’re free to go at your own pace, a good baseline for elliptical workouts is 15-20 minutes. As you get more comfortable and build your endurance, you can increase your speed, resistance, and incline (if your machine has variable incline settings).

We asked Matt Petrillo, C.S.C.S., director of adult fitness at The Annex Sports Performance in Passaic, N.J., how to get a great workout on the elliptical.

It has been revealed that “My clients utilize ellipticals through low-intensity interval training. To do this, choose a work interval ranging from 30-90 seconds and a rest interval between 30-60 seconds, making sure your work period is longer than your rest,” Petrillo claims.

He says when you are in your work period, you want to begin each round with your heart rate as close to 120 beats per minute as possible. By the end of your work period, you want your heart rate to be between 150-160 beats per minute.

It has been revealed that “During your rest period, the goal is to drop your heart rate to as close to 120 beats per minute as possible,” indicates Petrillo. Don’t have a heart rate monitor? That’s OK, too. “Simply go at the fastest sustainable pace you can while only breathing through your nose during your work periods,” Petrillo says.

Depending on fitness level and time constraints, go through the work/rest process for 15-30 rounds. “This type of workout helps build our aerobic system, which can greatly improve our cardiovascular and overall health,” Petrillo says.

To help you choose the best elliptical for your needs and goals, we evaluated dozens of machines and looked at several factors, including:.

According to recent reports, the flywheel is the heavy, rotating wheel inside your machine. It provides stability and momentum while you pedal. A heavier flywheel offers a better, smoother ride and is generally more expensive.

Industry observers note that A range of resistance levels is important for workout intensity variability and training progression. Ellipticals function on a fixed track, so increasing speed is limited.

You’ll want an elliptical with enough resistance options for challenging workouts as your physical fitness improves.

Incline ranges on an elliptical are more of an added bonus than a must-have. They can add a level of variability to training. By increasing or decreasing the slope, you activate different muscle groups and change the intensity of the workout without necessarily changing speed or resistance. As the slope increases, more output is required from the user to generate speed, which will increase heart rate. It’s similar to walking up a hill versus walking on flat ground.

Stride length refers to how far apart the pedals move from one another when in use. The stride length most affects how comfortable and natural the stride feels for you. A short stride length will feel cramped to anyone with longer legs or particularly long strides. Conversely, a large stride length may feel awkward and clunky to someone with short legs. There is no universal best stride length since it’s highly dependent on your leg length and overall height. Most ellipticals feature a 20-inch stride length, which works for the vast majority of owners.

Industry observers note that if you live in a small apartment or are equipping a tiny home gym space, you’ll want a compact elliptical that occupies minimal real estate. Measure out the space where you strategy to use your elliptical before you start your search.

Industry observers note that if you’re a sucker for technology and place a premium on programming with top-of-the-line features and conveniences, make sure you find an elliptical that checks off all your boxes. Write out a list of your must-have technology specifications and features before you begin your search. This will help you narrow down your focus and streamline the process.

This may seem like a no-brainer, but knowing your budget is imperative when buying any type of home exercise equipment. Ellipticals come at a variety of price points, from a few hundred dollars to several thousand.

Elliptical cross trainers are a great way to improve your cardio fitness and strength. The combination of the resistance from the pedals and handlebars provides you with a full-body workout.

Treadmills and elliptical trainers are great ways to get aerobic exercise. Choosing between them primarily depends on your fitness goals, your current fitness level, and whether you have an existing injury or condition that affects your joints or muscles. Consider these factors:-A full-size elliptical provides a full-body workout that targets your arms and shoulders in addition to your legs, calves, and glutes.-Ellipticals are not as high-impact since your feet remain in contact with the pedals rather than repeatedly striking the running deck of a treadmill. If you have joint pain or a lower-body injury, an elliptical will probably put less stress on those areas.-A treadmill makes more sense if you’re focused on building endurance and leg strength. It’s the better choice for runners and walkers.-The learning curve with an elliptical machine could be more difficult since it involves more complex movements than simply running or walking.Other factors besides workouts could also affect your decision. For example, treadmills tend to be more expensive than ellipticals. A high-quality elliptical trainer will almost certainly be less noisy than a treadmill, an important consideration for home workouts.

According to recent reports, how many calories you burn depends on your body size, fitness level, and the intensity and duration of your workout. However, according to Harvard Health Publishing, consumers can expect to burn between 270–370 calories for 30 minutes of exercise on an elliptical machine.

According to recent reports, yes, but not specifically. While it’s impossible to target fat burning in specific areas of your body, exercising on an elliptical machine, when paired with a weight-loss diet, can help users maintain a calorie deficit, contributing to all-over fat loss.

Consistency and accountability are crucial when it comes to weight loss. The best elliptical for weight loss is the machine you use regularly. Look for an elliptical with features to keep you motivated and focused. However, proper nutrition is just as important as having a consistent workout schedule.

Yes. The elliptical works both the upper body and lower body, targeting your glutes, quadriceps, hamstrings, calves, arms, and core.

Walking and the elliptical are cardio workouts. Typically, ellipticals enable you to burn more calories with varied intensities, resistance, and preset workout options. Ellipticals are easier on your joints than walking, offering a solid alternative to the impact of walking on pavement or a treadmill.

Seeing results from any form of exercise depends on your goals and the effort you put into your workouts.

The Best Creatine Supplements for Men for Muscle Growth and Enhanced Recovery

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that creatine is a popular muscle-building supplement, and for good reason.
  • There are tons of creatine supplements on the market, including powders, pills, and gummies.
  • According to recent reports, on one hand, having such a wide variety of options can be empowering.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that creatine is a popular muscle-building supplement, and for good reason. It’s one of the most research-backed supplements for muscle growth and recovery. While some people associate creatine with weightlifters or bodybuilders, it’s a great supplement for anyone looking to build muscle, enhance their performance, and promote better recovery.

There are tons of creatine supplements on the market, including powders, pills, and gummies. These supplements use various forms of creatine (more on that later), and some contain other ingredients that aim to help you grow muscle, recover faster, or sharpen your focus in the gym.

According to recent reports, on one hand, having such a wide variety of options can be empowering. On the other hand, it can be a challenge to figure out which is right for you.

In a recent development, to narrow down the field to only the best of the best, our expert product testers tried dozens of creatine supplements ranging from standard powders to convenient capsules to flavorful gummies. We looked for creatine supplements that taste good, mix well (when applicable), use quality ingredients, contain enough creatine per serving, and are affordable. Along the way, we spoke with certified personal trainers and nutritionists for guidance.

Below are our picks for the best creatine supplements for men. However, individuals of any gender can choose from this lineup with confidence.

According to recent reports, disclaimer: While this article is intended for educational and informational purposes, it should not be viewed as a substitute for medical advice. Furthermore, we intend the term “men” to include all men, including trans men. However, we understand most research on this topic has focused on cis men (men who are not trans). When we reference gender-based research and nutritional recommendations, we will clarify by saying “cis men.” We encourage trans and nonbinary people of all genders to consult with a trans-competent nutritionist regarding their supplements and training needs.

Sources indicate that transparent Labs Creatine HMB is our pick for the best creatine monohydrate because it contains 5 grams of it per serving, which is the researched-backed dose for improved athletic performance. “This dose is a great recommendation for the general population, but some sports nutrition recommendations recommend a dosage based on kilograms of body weight, so some individuals may require more than 5 grams to see a benefit,” states Anna Marie Clear, M.S., R.D., C.P.T.

Recent findings suggest that this dietary supplement contains β-hydroxy β-methylbutyrate (HMB), which the body naturally produces when it breaks down the amino acid leucine. Although more studies are needed, some research suggests HMB promotes muscle growth. “Leucine is the primary amino acid that triggers muscle protein synthesis,” Clear explains.”HMB and leucine are very similar, but research indicates HMB has no greater effect than leucine alone.”.

Transparent Labs also includes BioPerine, a derivative of black pepper that studies show increases nutrient bioavailability. “Bioperine may help enhance absorption of some nutrients, but research is limited on its impact alongside HMB and creatine,” indicates Clear.

In a recent development, earning a perfect formulation score of 5 out of 5 stars, Creatine HMB also received high marks from our testing team for taste. Although it fell shy of another 5-star rating, this supplement earned a solid score of 4 out of 5 in this all-crucial category.

According to recent reports, transparent Labs Creatine HMB comes in 13 flavors, including an unflavored version. This is a lot more flavor options than you’ll find in most creatine supplements and the most of any on our list.

Pete Nastasi, C.P.T., C.S.N.C., tried this supplement. “I’ve tried both the Blue Raspberry and Strawberry Lemonade flavors, which are sweetened with stevia extract, and both tasted great,” he says. “I love having a flavored creatine supplement in the morning before my morning workout.”.

However, while Nastasi liked the flavor, other testers say this supplement has a slightly bitter taste, which they attribute to the BioPerine.

In a recent development, “I tried Black Cherry and I wasn’t a huge fan of the taste of this one—it tasted a bit watered down, even with the right amount of water,” our product tester noted. “Some people may prefer this though!”.

While another tester also noted some tartness due to the BioPerine, she’s still optimistic about the Tropical Punch flavor.

“I bought this at the end of winter but I’m looking forward to drinking it in the summer because I find something refreshing about it that I think will be nice during the hotter months,” she explained.

Our team tested dozens of other creatines to come up with this list, with many of us relying on some form of this popular supplement for years. However, not every creatine product could make our list, so here are some honorable mentions that didn’t quite make the cut:.

It has been revealed that our team has tried more than 43 creatine supplements in total, with more added on the regular. We evaluate each supplement for the following factors:.

There are a few key factors you’ll want to consider when choosing a creatine supplement.

Sources indicate that research demonstrates the most efficacious dose of creatine is between 3 and 5 grams for most individuals. Look for supplements with servings within this range if you’re looking for maximum benefits, including increased muscle mass, faster recovery, and improved exercise capacity. Remember, larger individuals may require more creatine for maximum benefits—0.1 grams per kilogram of body weight is the research-backed recommendation.

Some supplements have additional ingredients to bolster the product’s effectiveness. Transparent Labs, for example, includes HMB, which some research highlights promotes muscle growth, though more research is needed. Legion includes L-carnitine, which research shows helps metabolize fat into energy. Consider your goals and whether or not you want a pure creatine supplement or one with other athletic performance-enhancing ingredients.

“I highly recommend collaborating with a sports dietitian to find the most optimal supplement for you based on your personal health, athletic, or physique goals and to ensure you are consuming an appropriate dosage from a safe and high-quality supplement,” states Anna Marie Clear, our expert reviewer and R.D.

It has been revealed that some creatine supplements use artificial ingredients and fillers to help improve taste and mixability. While many of the products on our list contain creatine as their sole ingredient, some, like Swoly gummies, use some artificial ingredients. Consider whether or not it’s key for your supplement to be completely pure.

Industry observers note that third-party testing is the best way to ensure that your supplement’s ingredients are pure and match what’s on the label. Supplements are not regulated by the FDA, so third-party testing gives consumers confidence in their products.

“It is also especially key to consider third-party testing for sport certifications from either Informed Sport or NSF Certified for Sport if you are a collegiate or professional athlete or if you are looking to compete in a weightlifting, bodybuilding, or other fitness competition to ensure you are consuming supplements free from banned substances,” says Clear.

Creatine phosphate (CrP) is a compound made of three amino acids: arginine, glycine, and methionine. The body produces creatine naturally in the liver, kidneys, and pancreas, with about 95% of it found in skeletal muscle. “Through diet, creatine is found primarily in red meat and seafood, however, to get an extra creatine boost, a creatine powder or pill supplement can help,” claims personal trainer and strength coach Will Duru.

Creatine supplies energy to muscles through the phosphocreatine system. “Creatine helps in the production of ATP (adenosine triphosphate)—the compound that provides energy to bodily processes such as muscle contraction,” nutritionist Rob Hobson notes. “Creatine can help with the production of ATP during maximum-effort exercises, such as sprints or intense muscular effort lasting between five and 10 seconds. It can also help recovery between exercise bouts.”.

Hobson says creatine can improve performance in sports involving repeated sprints, such as rugby or football, and high-intensity bursts, like track or swim sprints. “Creatine can also help you train harder through being able to do more work over a series of training sets,” he adds.

As a certified personal trainer, former rugby player, and longtime lifter, I can attest to the impact that creatine has on both performance and recovery. It’s been a staple in my supplement stack for years, and despite myths about unwanted weight gain and water retention, I’ve never experienced those side effects.

Recent findings suggest that as the most-researched supplement on the market, creatine has long been utilized by everyone from professional athletes to strength training enthusiasts to casual lifters. Let’s explore some of the positive potential effects of creatine supplementation:.

“Research reveals creatine supplementation helps muscle performance throughout a number of activities including soccer training, weight training, plyometric training, and even canoe training,” indicates Duru. Interestingly, this study also revealed that muscle power output and muscle strength still increased with creatine supplementation, even when research subjects didn’t do any exercise. This is in comparison to subjects who took a placebo supplement.

In a recent development, “There are lots of studies showing how creatine supplementation can improve strength, power, and high-intensity exercise performance. This is due to the role it plays in energy production and its ability to increase ATP availability during short bursts of intense activity,” indicates nutritionist Rob Hobson.

It has been revealed that want to build muscle? Creatine could be your go-to. “Creatine supplementation is often used to increase muscle mass. It can draw more water into your muscle cells, creating a cell volumization effect that may promote muscle growth,” says Hobson. “Additionally, creatine can enhance the effects of resistance training by increasing total muscle mass and strength gains.”.

According to a 2023 meta-analysis on the effects of creatine supplementation combined with resistance training, this protocol can promote “a small increase in the direct measures of skeletal muscle hypertrophy in both the upper and lower body.”.

Duru says for maximum muscle-building results, creatine loading can help. “The first time you take creatine, take around 20 to 25 grams of creatine every day for up to a week, broken up into 5-gram servings across the day. Then drop to the recommended 3 to 5 grams the day after this.”.

Clear adds: “If you are looking to initiate creatine supplementation with a loading dose of 20 grams per day, I recommend breaking this large dosage into smaller servings throughout the day to minimize gastrointestinal distress (i.e., diarrhea).”.

Sources indicate that recovery is key when training. Not only does it help you avoid injury, but a speedier recovery means we can get back to exercise quicker. Research shows creatine supplementation may reduce recovery time between spurts of intense exercise by reducing muscle damage.

Although supplementing with creatine does not entirely prevent muscle damage, studies show creatine reduces the immediate muscle damage that occurs after resistance training.

It has been revealed that studies show creatine can benefit brain function. “Creatine supplementation may have a beneficial effect on brain function, as the brain requires a significant amount of ATP for normal operation. It may be particularly beneficial in tasks requiring speed and quick thinking,” says Hobson.

Creatine supplementation is also important for overall health and wellness as you age. According to a 2021 study led by renowned creatine researcher Dr. Darren Candow, one year of creatine supplementation and resistance training had favorable effects on bone area and muscle density in older adults. This included both male and female participants, suggesting no differences between sex when it comes to creatine’s impact.

Sources indicate that not all creatine is created equal. In fact, there are multiple forms. Here’s a brief overview of the different types of creatine so you understand what to look for and what might suit you best.

Industry observers note that creatine monohydrate consists of creatine paired with a water molecule. As nutritionist Rob Hobson notes, this is the most research-backed form of creatine, and it’s typically the primary form used in most of the best-selling supplements in this category.

“Micronized creatine is processed to create smaller particles than the standard creatine powder,” Hobson says. “The intention of micronized creatine is to improve its solubility and absorption in the body so creatine is then used up by muscles more promptly.”.

It has been revealed that in this form, creatine is bound to ester salts, which some studies show makes the creatine more easily absorbed within the body. However, research shows creatine ethyl ester is not as effective as monohydrate.

It has been revealed that creatine nitrate is derived from the same molecule as creatine monohydrate but with a nitrate added. Some studies suggest creatine nitrate is more bioavailable than monohydrate, but results are mixed and more research is needed. Currently, creatine nitrate is only approved by the FDA at a daily dose of 750 milligrams per day.

This type of creatine is normally manufactured with added alkaline, so it has a higher pH than regular creatine monohydrate. However, research indicates there is little difference between buffered creatine and creatine monohydrate when it comes to training gains.

Recent findings suggest that A creatine loading phase involves taking a higher dose of creatine, typically between 20 and 25 grams, for up to a week, according to Duru. He recommends reducing to a dose of 3 to 5 grams a day after a week.

In a recent development, “A lot of people do a creatine loading phase to fully saturate the muscles when they first start taking creatine, and this can potentially speed up the benefits by a few days,” says Pete Nastasi, CPT, CSNC. “But if you take more than two to three days off from creatine, it’s likely that your creatine stores will go back down to baseline and you might want to do another loading phase,” he says. “That’s why I suggest people take it every day.”.

Studies show creatine loading phases (e.g. 20 grams per day for five to seven days) can help increase muscle creatine storage by 10 to 30 percent. However, creatine loading phases aren’t necessary. Studies show that long term, you can achieve the same effects without a loading phase. But if it’s speed you’re after, loading phases are a safe and effective way to quickly improve gains.

Studies show creatine supplementation is safe in both the short and long term for healthy individuals. Healthy people can safely take up to 30 grams per day for up to five years. However, as we’ll explain below, those with certain health conditions should avoid creatine supplements.

According to recent reports, “Since creatine is a safe supplement, there aren’t many precautions to take beyond sticking to the recommended dosage,” says nutritionist Rob Hobson. “Like all supplements, figure out if it is really necessary to suit your performance goals, as there is little point in taking it if it is not. If you are training for a marathon then it’s not really going to be of use to you but if you are looking to build more muscle and become stronger, then it’s a good choice.”.

Creatine works for most people, but those with certain pre-existing health conditions should avoid it. “Anyone with pre-existing kidney or liver conditions or impaired function should avoid creatine,” says Hobson. Experts say creatine supplements may prevent those with kidney or liver problems from producing their own creatine. “Anyone taking medications affecting kidney function should avoid creatine or speak to their GP first. This might include blood pressure medication or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs on a regular basis,” Hobson adds.

Hobson also advises against creatine supplementation for those younger than 18. “With adolescents, while the research suggests it may be okay for this age group, I avoid recommending it as the long-term effects are not fully understood yet,” he claims.

While myths exist about water retention, cramping, and even its legality, creatine is one of the most researched-backed supplements. If you’re a dedicated lifter looking to enhance your muscle gains, improve your performance in activities requiring short bursts of energy, or hasten your recovery, you shouldn’t hesitate to add one of the options from our list to your stack.

All you have to decide is whether you prefer a powder, pill, or gummy and you’ll be well on your way to unlocking the benefits of this uber-popular supplement.

Micronized creatine is processed to create smaller particles than the standard creatine powder. “Research shows micronized creatine monohydrate is not any more bioavailable than creatine monohydrate itself,” says R.D. Anna Marie Clear.

According to nutritionist Rob Hobson, most people take creatine after working out. “Research reveals taking creatine after your workout may be marginally more beneficial given the increased uptake by muscles during this period, as exercise increases blood flow to muscle tissue,” he indicates.Hobson recommends taking creatine with a meal or a drink containing carbohydrates. “The effects of insulin help transport creatine into muscle cells,” he says.

Sources indicate that in short, no. According to the International Society of Sports Nutrition, “There is no scientific evidence that the short- or long-term use of creatine monohydrate has any detrimental effects on otherwise healthy individuals.”.

Sources indicate that research indicates the best dose is from 3 to 5 grams per day for most individuals. However, as R.D. Anna Marie Clear notes, the research-backed dose of 0.1 grams of creatine per kilogram of body weight means some larger individuals will need more than 5 grams per day to see optimal results.

Creatine may help increase your lean skeletal muscle mass, which can, in turn, increase your overall body weight. This overall increase in lean body mass will likely improve your body composition, as creatine supplementation does not impact your fat mass. “Good quality randomized controlled trials (one week to two years in duration) show creatine supplementation does not increase fat mass. Acute creatine supplementation (seven days) had no effect on fat mass in young and older adults; however, fat-free mass increased.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, cold weather doesn’t have to mean putting your bike away until spring. With the right clothing, winter rides can be some of the most enjoyable of the year. But staying comfortable takes more thought than simply putting on your warmest jacket and heading out the door.

According to recent reports, the challenge is balancing warmth with breathability. Dress too lightly, and you’ll be cold and miserable. Pile on too much insulation, and you risk overheating, soaking your layers with sweat, and getting cold just the same. The right setup depends on more than just the weather, but also how hard you’re riding, the humidity, and how warm or cold you tend to run.

Recent findings suggest that after more than two decades of riding through the winter, I’ve learned that no single piece of clothing works for every ride. Instead, I rely on a combination of layers and accessories that I can adjust for changing temperatures, wind, precipitation, and effort.

Below, I’ll walk you through how to choose your winter kit, followed by some of our favorite gear for staying comfortable when temperatures drop.

According to recent reports, before I get dressed, I check the forecast as close to the start of the ride as possible. Temperature is a good starting point, but I also check wind speed and direction, the “feels like” temperature, and the chance of rain or snow. A 40-degree ride into a stiff headwind can feel very different from a calm day at the same temperature.

Recent findings suggest that next, think about the ride itself. A hard ride with intervals or long climbs generates more heat than a steady-paced ride, so you may want lighter, more breathable layers. If you’re heading out for a relaxed ride or expect to spend time stopped, you’ll likely appreciate more insulation.

Recent findings suggest that I generally aim to feel a little chilly when I first roll out. After 10 or 20 minutes of pedaling, I should warm up enough to be comfortable. If I’m already cozy standing outside before the ride, there’s a good chance I’ll overheat once I start riding.

Conditions can change during a ride, too. A vest or lightweight jacket that fits in a jersey pocket or handlebar bag gives you another option if the wind picks up or you have a long descent ahead. On rides with significant temperature swings, I’ll sometimes bring a second pair of gloves so I can swap to a warmer or lighter pair as needed.

According to recent reports, layering lets you adjust your clothing to the conditions instead of relying on one jacket to do everything. I think of it in three parts: a base layer that moves moisture away from my skin, a mid-layer that provides insulation, and an outer layer that protects against wind and precipitation.

Sources indicate that base layer: This sits closest to your skin and should fit snugly enough to move moisture away from your body. I typically start with a thin synthetic layer, even on cold days. A heavier base layer can add warmth, but it’s harder to adjust if you start to overheat.

Mid-layer: This is where you can add or subtract insulation for the temperature and your expected effort. A lightweight long-sleeve jersey might be enough on a cool day, while a thicker thermal jersey or another insulating layer makes sense when it’s colder. Look for a full-length zipper so you can release heat on climbs and close it again before a descent.

In a recent development, outer layer: A vest, softshell, or winter jacket protects you from wind and weather. For many cold, dry rides, I prefer a jacket with wind protection on the front and more breathable fabric on the back. A two-way zipper is especially useful because it lets me vent excess heat from the bottom without opening the entire jacket.

For steady rain, a waterproof shell provides more protection, but even the best rain jackets are less breathable than lighter layers. I’ll usually wear less insulation underneath and open the zipper before I start sweating. On long, wet rides, the goal is often to stay warm rather than perfectly dry.

Even if your core is comfortable, cold fingers or toes can cut a ride short. Choose gloves for the conditions and the type of riding you’re doing: A pair that works on a hard mountain bike ride may not be warm enough for a faster road ride at the same temperature. Fit matters, too. Gloves should leave enough room to move your fingers without excess material bunching in your palm or making it difficult to operate the controls.

For your feet, start with socks that fit comfortably inside your shoes, then add shoe covers for wind and cold. Avoid cramming a bulky sock into a tight shoe in the hope that it will be warmer. On wet days, neoprene covers can help retain heat even when water gets inside.

A cap that fits under your helmet helps protect your head and ears, while a neck gaiter can seal the gap at your collar. Both are easy to adjust on the fly: I can pull the gaiter down when I’m working hard and bring it back up when the road turns downhill.

The right combination takes some trial and error. Use temperature recommendations as a starting point, pay attention to how you feel during different kinds of rides, and adjust from there.

Sources indicate that these Assos gloves feel like they shouldn’t be this warm. But don’t let their thin, stretchy, low-bulk material fool you. These gloves have kept my hands toasty and comfortable into the high 30s, and I have mountain biked in them at near-freezing temperatures with no concerns.

They use soft fleece fabric inside and have an outer layer with excellent wind resistance. Assos also applies a water-repellent treatment to manage light rain and spray from damp roads. I’m a major fan of the palm of these gloves. They feature very minimal padding that helps with grip and bar feel. Fit and construction are excellent, with long cuffs to keep cold air out of your jacket, plus touchscreen functionality that works very well. The only knock against these gloves is their price. However, my personal pair is now in its fourth winter with no signs of wear, making these an easy recommendation if you want a good pair of gloves that will last.

At around $100, the Pearl Izumi Quest AmFIB is a great choice if you want a warm, simple jacket for winter rides without spending a lot or piecing together separate windproof and insulating layers. Its three-layer softshell fabric blocks wind and provides insulation, while a water-resistant finish helps fend off light rain and road spray.

Industry observers note that the relaxed fit leaves room for additional layers underneath, and the full-length zipper lets you vent some heat when you start to warm up. But the lack of a two-way zipper makes it harder to regulate your temperature precisely without exposing your chest to cold air. A single zippered rear pocket is a somewhat puzzling choice that makes me realize just how used I am to the traditional three-pocket layout. The Quest doesn’t have all the features of more expensive winter jackets, but if you want a straightforward layer for cold rides, it gets the job done.

According to recent reports, yes, the Velocio Luxe Thermal Bib Tights are expensive. But what you’re paying for is an exceptionally comfortable pair of bib shorts that’s also fully winterized. And after spending enough cold rides in tights with cheap chamois pads or fabric that bunches and chafes, I can tell you that skimping here can make winter riding uncomfortable in a whole new way.

Velocio also offers free repairs, which helps make the high upfront cost easier to justify if you plan to keep riding in them for many winters to come.

If I’m heading out for a ride in the rain, the Castelli Perfetto RoS 3 is the jacket I’m most likely to reach for. Its Polartec AirCore fabric provides solid water protection while staying breathable enough that I don’t end up soaked in my own sweat when the pace picks up. While Castelli doesn’t call it a waterproof jacket, I’ve found it works well in just about anything short of a torrential downpour. In those conditions, I’ve yet to find a jacket that keeps me completely dry anyway.

Pick the right base layer for the temperature, and the Perfetto can keep you dry and comfortable through a wide range of chilly, wet rides. Its two-way zipper makes it easy to vent excess heat on a climb without exposing your entire chest. When temperatures drop further, add a thermal mid-layer underneath. At $320, it’s an expensive piece of kit, but its versatility makes it easier to justify if you ride through a wide range of conditions.

It has been revealed that specialized’s Neoprene Shoe Covers are my favorite choice for cold, wet winter rides. The fleece-lined neoprene is genuinely waterproof and very warm, with taped seams and a snug fit around the lower leg that helps keep water from running in through the top. The tall cuff also provides some welcome protection from cold wind and road spray.

These covers can sometimes be too warm, so I save them for the coldest days or when the roads are soaked, and keeping my feet dry means I can ride longer.

Major glasses do more than you might think to make cold rides comfortable. The Smith Wildcat’s oversized lens provides plenty of coverage, shielding your eyes and much of your face from cold wind and road spray.

For winter riding, I’d choose the photochromic lens, which adjusts its tint as light conditions change. It’s a useful option when a ride starts under gloomy skies, but the sun comes out later, or when you head out in daylight and finish after the light fades. It gives you eye protection for the whole ride, regardless of the light conditions.

In a recent development, deFeet’s Woolie Boolie socks might have been one of the first pieces of cycling-specific gear I ever bought. When I started working as a bike messenger, I promptly learned what it felt like to spend a winter day riding around with cold feet. These wool socks were one of my first attempts at solving that problem.

In a recent development, the Woolie Boolie is a classic for a reason. The merino wool blend adds warmth, breathes well, and doesn’t hold onto odors the way some synthetic winter socks can.

In a recent development, the Velocio Alpha Zero is easily the warmest cycling jacket I’ve ever tested. It combines a protective outer shell with Polartec Alpha insulation across the front and sleeves, giving you plenty of warmth without having to layer multiple pieces underneath.

In a recent development, for me, it’s a jacket for the coldest winter rides. In fact, I find it’s probably too warm for anything above freezing. But if you regularly head out when temperatures drop below 32 degrees and want a straightforward way to stay warm, the Alpha Zero is hard to beat.

It has been revealed that pearl Izumi’s PRO Alpha Layer is one of my favorite ways to add warmth without sacrificing breathability. Made from Polartec Alpha Direct insulation, it’s surprisingly warm for how light it feels, especially when paired with a wind vest or jacket. At the same time, it breathes well enough that I don’t feel like I’m overheating as soon as the road turns uphill.

That combination makes it a versatile piece for winter riding. Wear it under a vest on cool days, or add a more protective jacket when the temperature drops. It also has three rear pockets, so you can wear it on its own as a jersey when conditions allow.

It has been revealed that ornot’s Micro Climate Jacket is a lightweight, packable wind jacket that’s useful on just about any ride where the weather might change. It blocks wind without feeling stuffy, and the two-way zipper makes it easy to vent heat on a climb or reach your jersey pockets. When you don’t need it, the jacket packs into its own rear pocket.

The fit is part of what makes the Micro Climate so versatile. Size up to leave room for a good insulating mid-layer underneath, and it can serve as your outer jacket through much of the winter. Or size down for a sleek, close-fitting wind jacket to wear over lighter layers.

Sources indicate that I’ve been using Pearl Izumi’s AmFIB Lobster Gloves for more than a decade. And they’re still one of the best gloves for when temps plummet.

Industry observers note that the gloves are made with 170g PrimaLoft Gold insulation, AmFIB soft-shell polyester-polyurethane fabric, and Ax Suede Laredo synthetic leather. It has the kind of exceptional warmth you’d get in a mitten. Yet the AmFIBs still allow for ample dexterity so you can operate both your shifters and brake levers. There’s also a gel palm pad for comfort while gripping the handlebar, plus touchscreen compatibility for the index finger and thumb.

In a recent development, test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a Upcoming York City bike messenger but swiftly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.
