Latest Update: This Winter I’m Turning to the CORE Temperature Monitor to Help Unlock My Strongest Season Yet

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1720 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bicycling

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review.
  • Industry observers note that I have been doing what I considered heat training for years—going on hard rides at the peak of summer heat and humidity.
  • This year I started to incorporate structured heat training into my routine—using the CORE body temperature sensor on rides outside as well as layered up rides inside on the trainer for active heat sessions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Industry observers note that I have been doing what I considered heat training for years—going on hard rides at the peak of summer heat and humidity. Riding in conditions that felt like I was riding into a hair dryer blowing hot and wet air into my face made me feel like I was checking off this heat training box. The reality is that I’ve been leaving performance on the table by not putting a little more structure around it.

This year I started to incorporate structured heat training into my routine—using the CORE body temperature sensor on rides outside as well as layered up rides inside on the trainer for active heat sessions. The CORE temperature monitor made it onto our gear of the year and has become an essential training tool for some of our team at Bicycling.

Like so many others, my time to ride has gotten more limited over the last few years—my schedule seems to be filled by work, family life, and more house projects than “free time.” Even with a packed schedule I was able to feel strong through multiple century gravel rides with more than 10,000 feet of climbing. I attribute a large piece of that base fitness to the weeks of heat training leading into those significant days in the saddle.

Next year I’m targeting my biggest days on the bike yet. I’ll be utilizing the CORE Temperature Monitor and newly introduced features in the app throughout my training to help get me there. Here we’ll go through the basics of heat training, differences between passive and active heat sessions, and why using the CORE sensor and app for your training this winter can give you the boost you need to hit your 2027 goals—whether those goals are staying strong, tackling your biggest ride, making it to the finish line, or stepping up the podium.

In a recent development, when done correctly, one of the major benefits of heat training is an increase in hemoglobin mass. I know, this isn’t a metric you’re used to seeing on your head unit or smartwatch. Consider this—when cyclists train at altitude camps one of their goals is to increase hemoglobin mass by the end of the camp. In short, increased hemoglobin mass can improve the blood’s ability to transport oxygen, which supports endurance performance, as well as potentially a higher VO₂ max.

Let’s be real—most of us aren’t going to be testing our hemoglobin mass at home to track progress. The good news is there are some easy ways you can see your progress throughout your heat training blocks. Aline Barre, Endurance Performance Lead at CORE, gave these three signals to look out for to watch your progress:.

Whatever your heat sessions look like, Barre noted to make sure you are staying appropriately hydrated for your fluid losses during your sessions and stop if you feel dizzy.

According to recent reports, the CORE temperature monitor is a small monitor that gets attached to your heart rate band. It can be put on an arm strap or chest strap, but I’ve only used it on my chest strap. When fitting the sensor on a chest strap, you need to set the sensor up so it lines up under your armpit against your torso. For me, this means I just have it set up on the side of the strap and I wear the heart monitor strap in the same place I did prior to adding the CORE monitor. The CORE temperature monitor gives people insight into their internal temperature during activity without being invasive—one previous tool was a rectal thermometer.

Recent findings suggest that the team at CORE has developed an app that pairs to the temperature monitor. It allows you to track your heat sessions, monitor your progress, and watch your heat training load go up during an active heat training session. Simply download it to your phone and you can access all your heat data there. I had a little bit more of a challenge installing the screen on my head units. Eventually I was able to get it set up as a screen on my different head units to monitor heat levels while riding outside.

Industry observers note that active heat training is when you are doing an activity, typically overdressed, to raise your body temperature while you are training. For cyclists this typically looks like putting on a few extra layers while you hop on the trainer. Just keep the fan off and watch your body temperature rise while you pedal.

It has been revealed that this is where the CORE sensor comes in. It demonstrates you how much your body temperature is rising to both keep it high enough for the target adaptations, and prevent it from tipping to an unsafe zone. “Athletes should spend about 45-60 minutes in CORE’s Heat Zone 3. This is the ideal zone for inducing physiological adaptations. More heat strain can overcook an athlete and less is not sufficient exposure,” states Barre. When I’m in heat zone three on the CORE app I typically sit around 101.5 degrees to 102.5 degrees.

Industry observers note that remember to bring plenty of fluids because you will more than likely be losing more sweat than you do on a typical trainer ride. During my heat sessions I typically sweat through all three layers and into my painter’s suit. You can weigh yourself before and after your ride to get an estimate of sweat loss. Typically, every pound of bodyweight lost equates to about 16 ounces of fluid loss. “Replace about 1.5 times [the lost] amount in total, before, during, and after the session,” indicates Barre. If you want to pick up another gadget to dial in your winter training, check out the Nix Biosensor to get a more accurate estimate of your fluid loss in a trainer session.

It has been revealed that “The ideal heat training set up is indoors where the climate can be controlled and there is no wind convection. The best protocol is to overdress with several non-permeable layers to trap heat against the skin, as heat strain is a product of both core and skin temps. Athletes should spend about 45-60 minutes in CORE’s Heat Zone 3. This is the ideal zone for inducing physiological adaptations. More heat strain can overcook an athlete and less is not sufficient exposure,” states Will Truettner, Head of Brand and Marketing at CORE.

There are still heat training benefits from passive heat training even though it does not appear to be as impactful as active heat training. Additionally, athletes like Reggie Miller swear by passive heat training, or sauna use, to support recovery. I’ve been using the Backyard Discovery Rylan Infrared Sauna for the last few months. While I can’t definitively say it’s a performance enhancer, I can say that I feel like I recover faster after building the sauna into my routine.

Just as with active heat training, start with shorter sessions and work your way up as you feel comfortable—and remember to hydrate. “Build up gradually—start with 10 to 15 minutes and add time each session,” claims Barre. One tip Barre gave to get the most out of your heat sessions is something I’ve started to incorporate into my own heat training days. “Do it right after training. Your core temperature is already high, which makes the passive session more effective. Keep the break in between as short as possible,” says Barre.

If you decide to add sauna sessions to your heat training block, then be sure to take your CORE temperature monitor off before you get in. You can add the passive training session to the app after you get out of the sauna. In the app you can select between options like standard sauna versus infrared, time and temperature in the sauna, and body temperature when you first got into the sauna. The different options will give you a different heat load score at the end.

Sources indicate that my first proper heat session was in my basement on the trainer. I layered up like I was on a New Year’s Eve ride in Michigan: thermal base layers, a warm midlayer, sweatpants, a hoodie, and a winter hat for a cherry on top. Here’s where it gets fun—I bought a painter’s suit on Amazon and cut it off at the knees so the suit legs didn’t get stuck in the cranks. I stuffed myself and all those layers into the painter’s suit and climbed on my trainer bike—without a fan. I pulled up Alp du Zwift, started pedaling, and I thought to myself, this will be interesting.

Recent findings suggest that it’s no surprise this is not the way to start heat training if you haven’t tried it before. I thought I’d be fine because I had two water bottles and I dropped in an extra bit of electrolytes—I was used to riding in the humid Latest Jersey heat, so I thought it would be no problem. By the top of the Alp du Zwift I knew I had overdone it.

Now, there’s a newly introduced coaching tool in the CORE app that can help prevent you from making the same mistakes I made when getting started. I’ve been trying the new feature in the app, and it makes progress easy by having a clear proposal for your goals. I chose to go with the building phase, which came out to five sessions per week where my target heat training load per session is five over the course of five weeks. I was able to put in a target date for when I want to have a proper base built up, and the coaching tool worked backward from there.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#182785. The Strongest Pre-Workout Powders to Fuel Your Training in 2025

📅 03 Mar 2025 • ⏱️ 25m • 📚 Deep Dive (4909 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Breakingmuscle ↗ Open Full Page

The Strongest Pre-Workout Powders to Fuel Your Training in 2025

📅 03 Mar 2025 | ⏱️ 25 min read (4909 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Breakingmuscle

⏱️ ~25 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that whether you’re starting your fitness journey or you’re a weightlifting junkie, there are several supplements that should be staples in your stack.
  • Not far behind would be another supplement that can help you achieve your muscle-building and weight-loss goals: pre-workout.
  • Recent findings suggest that however, just like not all barbells are created equal, neither are supps.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that whether you’re starting your fitness journey or you’re a weightlifting junkie, there are several supplements that should be staples in your stack. As a certified personal trainer and nutrition coach, I’d put a high-quality whey protein powder and one of the best creatines at the top.

Not far behind would be another supplement that can help you achieve your muscle-building and weight-loss goals: pre-workout.

Recent findings suggest that however, just like not all barbells are created equal, neither are supps. The strongest pre-workouts stand out from the pack because they are formulated with research-backed doses of four key ingredients — caffeine (at least 200 milligrams), L-citrulline (at least 4,000 milligrams), beta-alanine (at least 3,200 milligrams), and betaine (at least 2,500 milligrams) — for physical and mental performance enhancement.

To save you the trouble of sipping on something that won’t give you an effective muscle pump, our team of expert product testers tried more than 80 pre-workouts and reported which supplements delivered the most focus, power, and tingles. Then, with some guidance from a few other experts, our squad of CPTs, CNCs, CrossFit enthusiasts, and dedicated weightlifters narrowed down the list to the eight strongest pre-workouts so you can select the perfect match for your goals and preferences.

Medical disclaimer: This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If your goal is to improve your athletic performance and power output in the gym, then we recommend Transparent Labs BULK BLACK. This supplement contains a potent combination of 4,000 milligrams of beta-alanine, 2,500 milligrams of betaine anhydrous, and 10 other active ingredients. Beta-alanine, a nonessential amino acid, may improve potential power output by reducing muscle fatigue, allowing you to push out a few more reps while you exercise. And studies show betaine anhydrous may improve muscular endurance. These ingredients work together to enhance your training, paving the way for strength gains over time.

In a recent development, each serving of BULK BLACK also contains 350 milligrams of caffeine, which is close to the recommended daily limit of 400 milligrams. Overall, the impressive formulation earns 4 out of 5 stars from our team, as we docked a point for the high caffeine content since it may be too intense for some people.

However, this high-stim pre-workout is certainly effective.

According to recent reports, cory Kessler, C.P.T., C.F.N.C., has tried more than 25 pre-workouts. He tested the Blue Raspberry flavor of BULK BLACK before a cardio workout, noting that he felt more energized and focused throughout his workout. “I started sweating almost immediately, and within five to 10 minutes, I had a boost of energy, a massive pump, and felt like I could lift harder and stronger,” he says. Cory also experienced the tingling sensation common with high doses of beta-alanine.

It has been revealed that cory also enjoys using BULK BLACK before bodybuilding workouts since it contains 8,000 milligrams of citrulline malate. While more research is needed, some studies suggest citrulline malate may boost exercise and muscular performance.

Sources indicate that two other areas where BULK BLACK stands out: solubility and taste. Our team gave Transparent Labs perfect scores in both categories.

“BULK BLACK completely dissolved in my shaker bottle in only a few seconds with no clumps, grittiness, or residue,” Cory says.

Recent findings suggest that available in eight flavors ranging from Black Cherry to Watermelon Peach to Strawberry Mango, one of our other product testers chose the Blue Raspberry option, giving it 5 out of 5 stars for taste. However, there are some mixed reviews on Amazon about the taste, depending on which flavor you choose.

It has been revealed that “It’s hard to describe the taste of Blue Raspberry, but that’s exactly what it tastes like. Not too sweet, which is a good thing,” he says.

Related: Transparent Labs BCAA Glutamine Review.

Legion Pulse is our pick for the strongest natural pre-workout because it’s free from artificial sweeteners, flavors, and colors and contains six active ingredients that support enhanced energy.

As a CPT and CNC, I look for four main ingredients in a high-quality pre-workout supplement: caffeine, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, and L-citrulline. Each plays a key role in enhancing athletic performance. Research highlights:.

Sources indicate that legion Pulse contains all four, including 350 milligrams of caffeine per serving, which is very close to the recommended daily limit of 400 milligrams. Keep in mind that if you decide to try Pulse, it’s a good idea to monitor your caffeine intake from other sources like coffee or tea.

It has been revealed that “To get the most out of pre-workout supplements without stomach complications, start with a lower dose to see how your body reacts,” notes Dr. Christopher Mohr, Ph.D., RD. “Choose supplements with fewer stimulants if caffeine bothers you, or go for stimulant-free options.”.

Sources indicate that luckily, if you’re new to pre-workout or are caffeine-sensitive, you can also choose the non-stim version of Pulse. So, even though we’d like to see creatine in the formulation, we still give this a strong score of 4 out of 5 stars, especially since there’s a caffeine-free version.

One of our product testers has tried five different brands of pre-workout and puts Pulse atop her list because of its effectiveness.

Industry observers note that “I’ve been using Pulse three times a week for six months, and it always makes me feel energized and focused,” our tester states. “My goal is to improve my personal records and lift harder, so Pulse is my go-to when I train.”.

She reports that it typically takes 15 minutes for this high-stim pre-workout to kick in, and while it does give her tingles, it’s not overwhelming. “I never feel a drop-off, but rather a slow energy release,” she says.

Pulse comes in 22 flavors, including Pink Lemonade, Cherry Limeade, and Strawberry Kiwi, so there’s something to satisfy everyone’s taste buds. That noted, one of our testers gave Pulse 4 out of 5 stars for taste, noting that while it tastes sweet, there’s a “weird aftertaste.”.

Recent findings suggest that while the formulation and flavor options make this a top-rated pre-workout, Pulse is by no means a budget-friendly option. At around $45 for a 20-serving tub, it earns the lowest score of 1 out of 5 stars for price per serving.

Sources indicate that while many strong pre-workouts cost around $2 per serving, Nutricost Pre-X is our pick for the strongest budget pre-workout because it costs less than half of that. At about $0.93 per serving, one tester called it “the best value on the market,” and I agree, giving this a perfect score of 5 out of 5 for price per serving.

According to recent reports, although some budget pre-workouts lack key ingredients, Pre-X contains the four main ones we like to see in a pre-workout: caffeine, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, and L-citrulline. “The price is better than most other pre-workouts I’ve tried, especially for a supplement this good,” says one tester.

Each serving of Pre-X has 300 milligrams of caffeine and 4,000 milligrams of L-citrulline, so you should feel energized and get a good pump with this pre-workout. “I got a decent pump and had a calm focus without feeling overstimulated,” one tester notes.

Some testers say Pre-X has a slightly lower dosage of beta-alanine than some other pre-workouts on our list, but others say they experienced noticeable tingles during their workout.

Industry observers note that while testers did not experience any negative side effects when trying Pre-X, this pre-workout is made with the artificial sweetener sucralose. Some health experts have raised concerns about taking sucralose in high doses. As a CPT and someone who pays close attention to everything I put in my body, I tend to steer clear of artificial sweeteners. Because of this, we docked a point off the formulation score, giving Pre-X 4 out of 5 stars.

It has been revealed that nutricost Pre-X comes in five flavors, including Blue Raspberry, Peach Mango, and Watermelon. Collectively, our team gave this strong pre-workout 4.5 out of 5 stars for taste.

According to recent reports, “This tastes great ice cold or at room temperature. I look forward to drinking it before my workouts,” indicates one tester who tried Blue Raspberry.

Another tester who tried Peach Mango also gave Pre-X his stamp of approval.

According to recent reports, “No artificial sweetener taste at all. It has a nice flavor that’s not overly sweet.”.

Whether you like a strong pre-workout that’s sweet, sour, fruity, or tart, Jacked Factory NitroSurge has a fit for you. With 11 options, you can stick to your favorite or keep a few flavors in rotation to keep your taste buds on their proverbial toes. Between the deep lineup and satisfying flavors, NitroSurge earned a perfect score for taste.

One of our testers tried Strawberry Margarita, and let’s just say she was more than satisfied with her sipping experience.

Recent findings suggest that “It’s wildly delicious. I’d drink this by the side of the pool over ice all day.”.

Another tester prefers Jacked Factory NitroSurge to some other strong pre-workouts he’s tried. “I did not like the Pink Lemonade flavor of Legion Pulse, but I would definitely use the Grape NitroSurge again,” he indicates.

In a recent development, as for its effectiveness? For one of our product testers, it took about 20 minutes to feel NitroSurge kick in. At that point, he felt like he could lift harder.

“I usually work out in the morning because I feel most rested then, but even after taking this in the afternoon, I felt ‘jacked up’ and ready to go,” he notes, adding that he experienced tingles and a slight drop off, but neither was overwhelming.

According to recent reports, another tester who regularly takes strong pre-workouts doubled the dosage. He said he got “a bit of a boost from it” but nothing like what you’ll get from other strong pre-workouts. Ultimately, this makes NitroSurge a solid choice for beginners, as you can see how you respond to a single serving before upping it to two scoops.

Besides the taste, I like that it’s budget-friendly while still including evidence-backed ingredients, like L-citrulline, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, caffeine anhydrous, L-theanine, theobromine, and AstraGin. AstraGin, also found in Transparent Labs BULK BLACK, is a plant-based compound formulated to enhance nutrient absorption. While AstraGin is safe at 0.5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day, more research is needed on the potential performance-enhancing benefits.

Like some of the other pre-workouts on our list, NitroSurge is made with the artificial sweetener sucralose, which some health experts have raised concerns about taking in high doses. Also, Jacked Factory supplements do not undergo third-party testing, which ensures products include the ingredients listed on the label and nothing else. This is especially crucial for athletes who undergo drug testing for banned substances. We only gave Nitrosurge 3 out of 5 stars in this category since it is made in a Current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP)-certified and FDA-registered facility.

Recent findings suggest that for bodybuilders, a “pump” is a sign of a successful training session. Increased blood flow to the muscles makes them feel fuller and appear larger and more vascular during and after a workout. A pump also promotes muscle growth by delivering essential nutrients and oxygen to the muscles as blood flow increases. While you can achieve a pump through high-rep sets, drop sets, and supersets, high-stim pre-workouts like Gorilla Mode are specially designed to improve your pump.

According to recent reports, gorilla Mode contains several pump-enhancing ingredients in each scoop, including 5,000 milligrams of pure L-citrulline (more per scoop than any other pre-workout on our list) and 2,000 milligrams of Hydro Prime glycerol powder. L-citrulline works to widen blood vessels, increasing blood flow to the muscles. Glycerol powder is rapidly absorbed by the muscles and draws in water, which can cause muscle cell swelling.

Industry observers note that if you’re caffeine-sensitive or budget-conscious, this intense pre-workout may not be the best for you. Although one serving only contains 200 milligrams of caffeine, you will need to take two servings to get research-backed doses of some key ingredients, including creatine monohydrate (only 2.5 gram per serving). At that point, you’d be at 400 milligrams of caffeine, which is the total amount the FDA notes is safe for adults to consume per day. For this reason, we docked a point off the formulation, giving Gorilla Mode 4 out of 5 stars in this category.

Don’t forget that this also impacts how much bang you get for your buck. A 40-serving tub costs $60, and you’ll end up going through it that much quicker if you take two scoops before your training sessions. That would bring the cost to $3 per serving. So, from a value standpoint, we can only give Gorilla Mode 2.5 out of 5 stars.

On the other hand, this pricey supplement earned a strong score of 4.5 out of 5 stars for its effectiveness. One of our testers uses strong pre-workouts several times a week and tried Gorilla Mode before an upper-body workout. “Not only did I have a good pump, I also felt more focused. I knocked out a few more reps than usual during my workout,” he indicates. “I like the Fruit Punch flavor, although it was sweeter than I thought it would be.”.

It has been revealed that while our tester enjoyed Gorilla Mode’s taste, he says the powder was gritty and difficult to mix properly. This is likely due to the glycerol powder, which absorbs moisture, leading to clumping.

Recent findings suggest that if you like feeling skin tingles after taking your pre-workout, check out Crazy Nutrition Intensive Pre-Train. I love the prickly skin sensation because it lets me know my pre-workout is kicking in and it’s time to train. This temporary side effect, called paresthesia, is caused by beta-alanine, which works to increase muscular endurance.

It has been revealed that intensive Pre-Train has 3,500 milligrams of beta-alanine per serving, which is more per serving than almost all of the other pre-workouts on our list. “Beta-alanine is found in most pre-workout supplements, likely because it helps reduce fatigue and improve endurance in the short term,” states registered dietitian Alex Oskian. “This is because it reduces acidity in the body, which comes from lactic acid build-up.”.

Industry observers note that our product tester used Crazy Nutrition Intensive Pre-Train before a high-intensity interval training (HIIT) workout and felt the tingles within 15 minutes. “These were strong compared to some other pre-workouts I’ve tried,” he claims. “I felt good tingles in my hands and face, which lasted for about an hour.”.

In a recent development, earning a 5 out of 5 for effectiveness, Intense Pre-Train is also available in a caffeine-free version for those who don’t want stimulants in their pre-workout. The non-stim version comes in Green Apple, which our tester claims tasted more like a greens powder than a sour apple.

“I’m rather caffeine-dependent, so I didn’t feel a burst of energy. I prefer caffeinated pre-workouts, but this is a great option for a late-night lifting session,” she says. Other testers who tried the Fruit Punch flavor say they enjoyed the tangy taste. To enhance the flavor, Crazy Nutrition is sweetened with the artificial sweetener sucralose. With some mixed reviews on the different flavors, we give this pre-workout a 3.5 out of 5 for taste.

Sources indicate that onnit Alpha Brain is designed to increase mental acuity and focus. Testers say that’s exactly how they felt after trying Onnit Alpha Brain, which is why it’s our pick for the strongest pre-workout for focus.“What makes this pre-workout stand out is the cognitive effects. I felt significantly more focused after taking Alpha Brain than any other pre-workout I’ve tried,” says one of our testers.

Other testers agreed, saying Alpha Brain helped them feel present and ready to work out without being overstimulated, leading to an effectiveness score of 4 out of 5 stars.

Onnit Alpha Brain’s formula differs from most other strong pre-workout supplements on our list — it contains nootropics, substances that enhance learning and memory. One of the key ingredients, NooGandha, is an ashwagandha extract that can reduce stress and enhance well-being by reducing cortisol levels in the body.

Industry observers note that another key ingredient, AlphaSize, may promote the production of acetylcholine, a powerful neurotransmitter that enhances cognitive function. However, studies demonstrating the effect of alpha-GPC on cognitive performance used 200 to 400 milligram doses per day, and a serving of Onnit Alpha brain has 125 milligrams.

The other unique ingredient in Onnit Alpha Brain is Dynamine. It works similarly to caffeine, by blocking the body’s adenosine receptors that cause you to feel tired. However, this ingredient is banned in all sports supplements in Australia. While Dynamine is still allowed for sports competitions in the U.S., it is possible it will be banned in the future. Competitive athletes may want to steer clear of this product.

One of our testers states Alpha Brain is only middle-of-the-road compared to other strong pre-workouts when it comes to physical energy. “After taking other strong pre-workouts, I usually experience a boost in energy. After taking this pre-workout, the mental effects were much more noticeable than the physical ones,” she says. That may be in part because Alpha Brain lacks ingredients like betaine anhydrous, taurine, and creatine, which can support muscle growth and recovery.

According to recent reports, we give the formulation 4 out of 5 stars thanks to the inclusion of nootropics, which are swiftly becoming more prevalent in the supplement market. But be aware that this probably isn’t your best bet for boosting your physical energy levels.

Recent findings suggest that long before the days of gummy and ready-to-drink (RTD) pre-workout options, the most popular choice was the original C4. The latest version, C4 Ultimate, is more concentrated than the classic formula, combining both exercise performance and cognitive-enhancing ingredients.

One of our testers tried C4 Ultimate before a 30-minute HIIT workout, reporting that the caffeine blend got her zoned in before her training.

“I felt great throughout the entire workout,” she reported, giving C4 Ultimate a perfect score for effectiveness.

This high-stim pre-workout is sweetened with sucralose, which some health experts have raised concerns about. While our tester doesn’t mind a very sweet pre-workout, the Icy Blue Razz flavor was a little too sugary for her liking. Mixing it in more water than recommended balances out the sweetness.

However, another tester was blown away by the Sour Batch Bros flavor, saying it tasted “just like Sour Patch Kids.” Taking both of their experiences into consideration, we’ll meet in the middle and give C4 Ultimate a 4 out of 5 for taste, especially since it comes in multiple flavors.

Another plus for this product: It contains creatine — a popular supplement among athletes and bodybuilders for its ability to boost strength, enhance recovery, and prevent injury. Because of its performance-enhancing capabilities, some people like to take creatine in addition to their pre-workout. If you want the best of both worlds, we recommend C4 Ultimate.

Keep in mind that one serving contains 1.5 grams of creatine per serving, which is less than the recommended value of 3 to 5 grams daily. If you want to get the most performance-enhancing benefits from creatine, you should invest in a standalone supplement to help support your fitness goals.One final note: If you compete in a sport that requires drug testing, C4 Ultimate may not be the best strong pre-workout for you because it’s made with Dynamine, which is currently banned for use in Australia.

Recent findings suggest that our team of expert testers includes certified personal trainers, nutrition coaches, and CrossFit enthusiasts. As dedicated lifters and lovers of all things health and fitness, we’ve collectively tried more than 80 pre-workouts, giving us a broad perspective of what’s available on the market.

We tested each supplement before a workout, and in some cases, for several weeks or months, to evaluate its performance-enhancing benefits, taste, and whether the supplement had any negative side effects.

Using a 1-5 scoring system, we rated each pre-workout on a variety of factors, including:.

At the end of the testing period, we compared feedback to whittle our list down to only the best of the best. We also received valuable input from nutrition experts on what makes a strong pre-workout.

Recent findings suggest that A strong pre-workout contains a combination of performance-enhancing ingredients in research-backed dosages. “Usually, the strength of a pre-workout is based upon the amount of stimulants it contains. High doses of caffeine (300+ milligrams) are usually a quick identifier of the pre-workout’s strength,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian states.

However, the potency of a pre-workout goes beyond the caffeine content. Other active ingredients like L-citrulline, beta-alanine, and betaine anhydrous can impact energy, focus muscular endurance, and power output.

In a recent development, “Stronger via the amount of caffeine isn’t always better. If the goal is a bigger pump in the gym, other ingredients like L-citrulline may be better,” says Alex. “Another common ingredient that can help a pre-workout feel stronger is beta-alanine, which may cause a tingling or ‘pins and needles’ sensation on the skin.”.

It’s also crucial to remember that “strong” is a subjective term. For example, I can handle a full scoop of RedCon1 Total War without a problem, but I have friends who get too many tingles from a single serving.

Recent findings suggest that “Everyone’s body reacts differently to various compounds, so what works for one person might not be best for another,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, Ph.D., RD.

A strong, well-dosed pre-workout supplement may help you train harder by boosting your energy, focus, and endurance during intense workouts.

“There are a few things that are really helpful when you are looking for a great gym session: energy to do the work, mental clarity to help focus on what you are doing (not just to work the muscle, but to prevent injury), and a great workout,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian says. “Using a pre-workout may just help you achieve all of these.”.

Let’s explore the potential benefits of taking a strong pre-workout before you start your training session.

In a recent development, caffeine is one of the most popular stimulants used in pre-workout supplements to enhance energy levels and improve focus. Almost all of the pre-workouts on our list use caffeine and L-theanine. Studies have shown when paired with caffeine, L-theanine may improve cognitive performance.

“Most pre-workouts contain the stimulant caffeine in higher dosages. L-theanine helps counteract the unwanted effects of caffeine supplementation: jittery feelings and a post-caffeine crash,” Alex claims. “You might see less mental fatigue, improved reaction time, and fewer headaches while regularly supplementing with L-theanine.”.

I like taking a pre-workout to improve my focus because it helps intensify my workout and keep me #lockedin. Several pre-workouts on our list contain Alpha-GPC and tyrosine to give you that zoned-in feeling. Research suggests Alpha-GPC may improve cognitive function, and tyrosine may increase dopamine levels and cognition. One study found L-tyrosine helped improve people’s memory while they worked on a demanding task.

It has been revealed that A pre-workout may help you squeeze out a few more reps as you work to build strength and muscle. Two ingredients commonly used in pre-workout, beta-alanine and betaine anhydrous, may help reduce fatigue and support muscular endurance.

“Research suggests betaine anhydrous can improve muscle strength and power via increased total work capacity and improved protein synthesis within the body. Simply put, you can do more work, which leads to increased strength and muscle growth,” says Alex.

Another common ingredient, taurine, may improve your performance and power.

Registered dietitian Alex Oskian says not every pre-workout is created equal, so it’s notable to pay attention to what’s on the label. “Supplements are not regulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This means the supplement might not contain all the ingredients you’re looking for and may even contain unwanted ingredients,” she says. Alex recommends looking for supplements that undergo third-party testing.

If you choose a high-stim pre-workout, be mindful of your caffeine intake from other sources like coffee, tea, or soda so that you don’t go over the daily recommended value of 400 milligrams. This will help prevent potential negative side effects like jitters, anxiety, or trouble falling asleep.

“Consuming caffeine at the end of your day may cause sleep disturbances, which only hurts performance in the long run,” claims Oskian.

Recent findings suggest that no matter which pre-workout you choose, it’s vital to follow the recommended intake guidelines. Remember, pre-workouts should not be taken more than once per day.

“Pre-workout supplements are generally safe for healthy adults, but they can have some potential side effects,” states Dr. Raj Dasgupta, MD, FACP, FCCP, FAASM. “It is important to start with a low dose and talk to your doctor before taking them, especially if you have any underlying health conditions.”.

There are a number of important factors to consider when deciding which strong pre-workout is right for you, including:.

Many strong pre-workouts incorporate a variety of active ingredients. When choosing a pre-workout supplement, consider your goals. For example, a bodybuilder may prefer a pre-workout powder that’s highly caffeinated and contains ingredients such as L-citrulline, betaine anhydrous, and creatine to help improve performance. On the other hand, an endurance athlete may want a pre-workout that has less caffeine but includes beta-alanine, BCAAs, and mineral electrolytes.

Recent findings suggest that whenever possible, I choose supplements that are tested by a third party for purity and have transparent labeling. Athletes who undergo drug testing should look for certifications from Informed Choice and NSF, which ensure the product does not include any banned substances.

Recent findings suggest that although we test all of the products we recommend, it’s important to check out customer reviews, especially from people with similar fitness goals and preferences. They can provide valuable insights into the product’s overall effectiveness, potential side effects, and the most popular flavors.

It has been revealed that “Recommended brands and products are ones that are highly rated by users and contain ingredients that have been backed by scientific research,” says Dr. Raj Dasgupta.

“Taste plays a substantial role in pre-workout selection. If you don’t like a particular flavor, then you likely won’t drink the pre-workout no matter its benefits,” Oskian says. It’s also important to consider the use of artificial flavors, colors, and sweeteners.

According to recent reports, the price of a pre-workout doesn’t necessarily reflect its effectiveness. Understanding the ingredients list and dosage levels is important to ensure you’re paying for a high-quality supplement and not just expensive marketing.

There are a few potential red flags you want to avoid when picking out a pre-workout.

In a recent development, I like to avoid supplements made using proprietary blends. These blends are combinations of ingredients, but the individual doses are not fully disclosed. This lack of transparency makes it impossible to assess the effectiveness and safety of the supplement.

Many fitness enthusiasts and athletes prefer all-natural ingredients and products free from unnecessary fillers or additives. “If sugar alcohols and artificial sweeteners wreak havoc on your stomach, make sure those aren’t on the ingredient list,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian states.

Athletes who compete in sanctioned organizations should make sure the supplements they use are third-party tested and certified banned substance-free.

It has been revealed that if you have big fitness goals, choosing a strong pre-workout formulated with safe and effective doses of science-backed ingredients is worth it to deliver performance-enhancing effects. Keep in mind that even the strongest pre-workouts on the market won’t make you run faster, lift heavier, or exercise longer on their own. These supplements are designed to help you put in the work at the gym to make gains and enhance your performance over time.

Sources indicate that ultimately, though, a strong pre-workout is only part of the equation to becoming the strongest version of yourself. At the end of the day, you have to put in the work, follow a sound nutrition strategy, and prioritize rest and recovery to crush your fat-burning and muscle-building goals.

Yes, technically, you can take a pre-workout made with 400 milligrams of caffeine. However, that is the maximum daily dose recommended by the FDA. This means if you’re using a high-stim pre-workout, you may want to avoid caffeine from other sources like coffee, tea, soda, or energy drinks. Since 400 milligrams is the maximum recommended daily dose, I do not advise using a pre-workout containing 600 milligrams of caffeine.

It has been revealed that A pre-workout can directly and indirectly make you stronger. A well-dosed pre-workout may help you add a few pounds to your lifts or allow you to push out a few more reps during your workout. However, real strength gains will come from consistent training, proper nutrition, and recovery. If a pre-workout supplement helps you stay consistent in the gym, it may also help you gain strength and muscle mass.

Industry observers note that yes. Depending on your sensitivity to stimulants like caffeine, you may experience side effects, including jitters, anxiety, or difficulty falling asleep. If this is the case, use a half serving or a more moderately dosed pre-workout to assess your tolerance.

#182784. Like Jess McClain, I Took Time Off From Running—and Came Back Stronger. These Signs Mean It’s Time to Step Away.

Like Jess McClain, I Took Time Off From Running—and Came Back Stronger. These Signs Mean It’s Time to Step Away.

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1688 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Runnersworld

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that they say distance makes the heart grow fonder, and that’s true for me with running.
  • According to recent reports, around this time last year, I went from lifting two to three days a week while training for my first marathon to stopping workouts completely and struggling to get off my couch.
  • Industry observers note that professional distance runner and Latest York City Marathon runner-up Jess McClain previously told Runner’s World she felt similarly about six years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that they say distance makes the heart grow fonder, and that’s true for me with running. But by “distance,” I don’t mean bumping up my mileage or running farther. I mean taking time and space away from my sport during seasons when I feel burned out, lost, or simply exhausted.

According to recent reports, around this time last year, I went from lifting two to three days a week while training for my first marathon to stopping workouts completely and struggling to get off my couch. The second I crossed the finish line, all I wanted to do was let my running shoes collect dust, avoid my local trail, and avoid stepping foot in the gym for a while.

Industry observers note that professional distance runner and Latest York City Marathon runner-up Jess McClain previously told Runner’s World she felt similarly about six years ago. At that time, she consistently stopped hitting her paces in her workouts and decided to step back from running—a break that lasted about two years.

In a recent development, in my case, I wasn’t as decisive. For months, I resisted the idea that I needed to take a break.

I’d heard that a month is generally how long you need to recover from a marathon, so I told myself that’s when I would jump into winter base training. But every time I tried to get back out there, I got bored and I struggled to recover from my runs. I waited until summer for the urge to work out again, but it never really came back.

Sources indicate that for a while, I felt like getting burned out was my fault, that I must have pushed too hard in training. Looking back now—and with help from an expert—I understand that my break was exactly what I needed to get back to my sport in a sustainable way.

According to recent reports, my break from running lasted about nine months, and I came back feeling like the runner I had always been before. Plus, I raced one of my fastest half marathons as my comeback.

Below I offer the telltale signs it’s time for a break from running, what a “break” really means, and the benefits you can gain from stepping away from the sport for a while—even if it seems impossible to do so at first.

According to recent reports, the farther away I got from my training cycle, the more I realized how much I overtrained. I’d been strength training for 90 minutes three times a week with heavy weights while balancing 30-plus-mile weeks and 20-mile long runs. As I gained more perspective after my race ended, I noticed signs that I was in desperate need of a break.

“Pay attention to trends and patterns [throughout your training],” Erin Ayala, PhD, a sports psychologist, certified mental performance consultant, and founder of Skadi Sport Psychology, tells Runner’s World. “We all have bad days where the numbers aren’t coming together or a run feels harder than it normally does at a given pace. But if it continues to occur, then it can definitely be a sign to take a break,” she states.

In a recent development, ayala says there are three main factors that often lead to athletic burnout. Here’s what each can look like, and how I experienced them.

You might need to take a step back if you find yourself hitting training plateaus despite putting in your best efforts.

I picked a training plan that included paces far too fast for my fitness level at the time, so every interval workout I did felt difficult, and my paces never really improved. The longer the intervals got, the farther I was from my desired split. But I kept checking off the weekly workouts anyway.

This lack of personal achievement and growth can halt your motivation levels. “When you’re not able to progress and you lose sight of [personal achievements] you’re just going through the motions, that’s a really massive red flag,” Ayala claims.

After the first month or so, marathon training started to feel more like a chore and I felt really tired and disconnected during my workouts. I figured it was probably normal because I had never run a marathon before, but it turns out that’s not how you should expect to feel daily in your training. “If the workouts are just a grind and you’re having to peel yourself off of the couch in order to get them in, and that’s a sustained pattern, then that’s another massive red flag,” Ayala says.

According to recent reports, A change in my relationship with running and my “why” meant grappling with my identity as a runner, which Ayala indicates is the third factor that can contribute to athletic burnout. You might ask yourself questions like, “Why do I even do this anymore?” and “What’s the point?” She says that if those questions linger for more than a week or so, then that’s a sign you might need a break.

In a recent development, by the time I got to the start line, I questioned why I was even there, and all I could do was get through it. “There’s a very real sense of grief and loss, and that’s really scary,” when taking a step back from running, Ayala explains. “Often we hang on quite desperately to our athletic identity when it’s also okay to move on and to do something different.”.

Once I knew I needed a break from running, I didn’t quite know how to hit pause.

Sources indicate that then Ayala pointed out that perfectionism can affect your relationship with your sport. And simply hearing that helped me realize why I needed to step away.

There are two types of perfectionists, Ayala explains. The first type is the high achiever, who wants to be the best and perform at the top as much as possible. The second type of perfectionist takes a more “maladaptive form.” These individuals are highly motivated by others’ perceptions and expectations, she claims. They might fear failure and generally don’t want to disappoint people.

In a recent development, that second type of perfectionism resonated with me because I realized I was listening to a nagging voice in my head that expected me to give absolutely everything I had to my training. And if I didn’t, I would face that critical voice’s judgment and let it fill me with disappointment and shame.

“Breaks can be helpful because they essentially force you to turn that perfectionistic tendency off. They’re a good way to keep yourself balanced,” Ayala adds.

Once I knew this and decided to take a break, I figured out how to fill my time.

According to recent reports, those first few months after marathon training, I was so excited to not think about running at all. Instead, I looked forward to filling my free time by rebooting my old Webkinz account (an online virtual-pet game popular in the mid-2000s), decorating my newly introduced apartment, and watching a lot of TV.

Sources indicate that “First, just give yourself time. Then, you can create other bite-sized goals like daily movement, getting outside, spending time with friends, or exploring different hobbies,” Ayala suggests.

In a recent development, when I passed the two-month mark of my break, I took up pottery classes. While that hobby didn’t last, it gave me the space I needed from running.

I knew, deep down, that rest was probably what I needed. But when I took time off, I felt too anxious and ashamed to even enjoy it: I kept thinking about how much time I was wasting and how out-of-shape I felt. “The problem [with athletic burnout] isn’t that you just need to motivate yourself harder. You need to rest in order to get that intrinsic motivation back,” Ayala says.

Ayala explains that if we lose our intrinsic motivation, we often rely on feelings of shame and discipline to keep up with our routine, which ultimately isn’t sustainable.

When I was honest with myself, I found my new “why” for running—my intrinsic motivator—and that was because of how strong, creative, and capable it makes me feel.

Industry observers note that one piece of advice from Ayala especially resonates with me: Accept where you’re at and normalize taking a break. “I would argue that getting burned out is a very normal and expected part of being an athlete,” she says. “If you are an athlete long enough, you are going to get burned out at some point and that’s okay. It doesn’t mean that you’re doing something wrong.”.

Once I accepted that I was dealing with a longer-term case of burnout and some depression, I began to see light at the end of the tunnel. I set bite-sized goals, per Ayala’s suggestion, and began by committing to running just five minutes a day for a month. With that, running clicked for me again.

According to recent reports, looking back on my time away from running, I don’t view it with shame or anxiety anymore. I see it as both a period of my life when I learned about myself as an athlete and about how my brain works. It was also a time of physiological and mental recovery from so much training stress.

By stepping away, I unlocked a upcoming life experience that can help inform me if—and probably when—I experience burnout again. That perspective shift alone lifts so much weight off my shoulders.

Plus, I’ve come back to the sport now feeling refreshed. I ran one of my fastest half marathons and feel ready to tackle another training initiative. I have the drive to set and achieve goals again. And that’s an irreplaceable benefit to taking some time away.

Kristine Kearns, a writer and avid runner, joined Runner’s World and Bicycling in July 2024. She previously coached high school girls cross country and right now competes in seasonal races, with more than six years of distance training and an affinity for weightlifting. You can find her wearing purple, baking cupcakes, and visiting her local farmers market.

Even though I finally embraced wearing leggings last year, I still hesitate when it comes to winterizing my running gear—even when the “feels like” temp is 28 degrees Fahrenheit on a 34-degree day. The simplest gear that transforms my getup, doesn’t make me regret overdressing, and helps me stay warm when the weather begins taking its nippy turn? Gloves. My pair of choice is the Smartwool Active Fleece Insulated.

Industry observers note that of all the runs and races I’ve underdressed for, the one accessory I always regret not putting on is a pair of gloves. I’m the kind of person whose hands are constantly cold. (Healthcare friends, I’m sorry for having fingers that refuse to get a quick oxygen read.).

I could go the mitts route, and I do when I need an extra layer over my gloved fingers (yes, I double up). But the thing about running, especially when you’re training for Boston in the spring, is that you need to be able to spread your 10 digits and use them to retrieve fuel—or lip balm or a Kleenex—from the depths of your pockets, which requires more dexterity than mittens allow.

Recent findings suggest that I like Smartwool’s gloves because of their range of sizes, though I will admit the extra small is still slightly long in the tips due to their unisex sizing. The gloves are double-layer knit and have a blend of merino wool and polyester to thermoregulate your hands and wick away sweat. The overlay panels serve as windproof protection.

Besides warmth and the usage of my fingers, the Active Fleece also provides visibility, thanks to a reflective logo and piping on the back of the hand. Being seen is important when daylight hours are shorter and I need to log that run before dawn or can only fit in a workout at dusk.

Industry observers note that the index and thumb have touchscreen-compatible pads. I wouldn’t recommend them for long-winded texts since, through my own experience, messages aren’t always accurate. But it’s nice that I can type into Google Maps or use dictation and send, “PICK ME UP—I MADE A HORRIBLE MISTAKE” with a location pin.

Industry observers note that sometimes the best test is when you’re not running. On our first chilly morning this fall, I got up early on a Sunday and waited to cheer at mile 10 of a half marathon. The precursor to the waiting was pacing every block in a half-mile radius, trying to figure out if I was actually on the race course.

When the runners came in and I finally found the right sidewalk corner, the stutter in my voice told me I should have worn two extra layers. Despite my frozen core, I was surprised I still had the feeling in my Smartwool gloved hands.

The best part of that morning besides being able to type out post-cheer coffee shop directions? Sticking it out so I could encourage runners with more cowbell.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As with many things in life these days, it all started with an episode of the Peter Attia podcast.

It has been revealed that in this edition, our nation’s most Badass Doctor was interviewing a guest I initially dismissed as not overly applicable to my own lifestyle. A young,excessively handsome dude who happened to be a writer with a newly introduced book out. But the headline of the episode was just intriguing enough to get me to click.

Wow, what an amazing turn of phrase, and what a concise summary of the core of this whole Mustachianism thing I’ve been trying to express for the past dozen years.

While the news headlines cry constantly about our nationwide personal debt crisis or health crisis or any other number of things that suggest that life is so hard these days, I have always seen the opposite: on average, we Americans seem to have a problem of ridiculous overindulgence and easiness in our lives, and our main problem is not recognizing it, and the damage it does to us.

Recent findings suggest that so of course I had to click, and then listen to the whole two hour episode, and then buy the book, and then spend the past month reading and digesting it in small, meaningful chunks like the modern-day chunk of scripture-like wisdom that it is. And wow, am I glad I did so.

The author is Michael Easter, a former writer for Men’s Health magazine was also once catastrophically addicted to alcohol – and descended from a long family line of ancestors with the same affliction.

It has been revealed that he was lucky to catch himself from that fall in time to save his own life, and that story alone makes the book worth reading as someone who has stood by helplessly as loved ones battled with addiction. But I think his history with overindulgence in the hollow comforts of alcohol also gives him an edge on writing about the battle between comfort and hardship on the bigger stage of life in general.

So what is The Comfort Crisis about, and how can it make all of our lives better?

Recent findings suggest that the best part about this book is just what a damned good writer this Easter guy is. Like many of the most fun popular science books*, it follows a split narrative which jumps back and forth to interweave the story of an insanely difficult caribou hunting trip he joined in a remote pocket of Alaska, with the appropriate bits of science, psychology and cultural commentary that help us explain and learn from each chapter of the epic shit he had just endured. This allows us to process and apply the lessons in our own lives.

For example, have you ever wondered why the type of bored, rich suburbanites who populate the board of your local Homeowner Association and whine about unacceptably tall weeds or unauthorized skateboarding on Nextdoor are so insufferable?

Why can’t they do something better with their time?

It turns out that there’s a scientific explanation for these unfortunate people, along with most of our other problems:.

The tendency of humans to always scan our environment for problems, regardless of how safe and perfect that environment is.

The book cited a study in which researchers told people to look for danger, in an environment which gradually became safer and safer:.

“When they ran out of stuff to find they would start looking for a wider range of stuff, even if this was not conscious or intentional, because their job was to look for threats.”.

“With that in mind, Levari recently conducted a series of studies to find out if the human brain searches for problems even when problems become infrequent or don’t exist.“.

“As we experience fewer problems, we don’t become more satisfied. We just lower our threshold for what we consider a problem.“.

In other words, even when our lives are virtually problem free, instead of appreciating our good fortune we just start making up shit that we can complain about instead.

Sources indicate that and then our politicians cock their greasy, finely-tuned ears in our direction and make up policies to appease our mostly-insubstantial concerns. And they invent their own trivial “wedge” complications to get us to all bicker about our different cultures and religions, suddenly caring about things that would not have even been problems if nobody told us they were.

And there’s America’s weakness in a nutshell, and meanwhile our strength comes entirely from the times we choose not to waste our time stooping to this level.

Meanwhile, the opposite effect holds true: people who survive in rougher environments than us end up more resilient and less prone to complaining.

In a series of recent interviews, Ukrainian people living in the war zones of their occupied country were asked “is it safe to live where you live?” and a strangely high percentage still remarked “Yes” – not all that different from the responses of US residents when asked the same question about their own cities.

This adaptation principle also explains why some first generation immigrants tend to build businesses and wealth while their own offspring in second and third generations are more likely to become complacent and spend it down. As an immigrant myself, I can see why this is: conditions were just slightly more harsh and less comfortable and wealthy where I grew up, so I adapted to those conditions as “normal” which made the United States seem posh and easy by comparison. Which made it easier to spend less money and accumulate more.

The trap of pointless worry is just one of the many revelations of The Comfort Crisis. It also gives insightful explanations for why spending time in Nature boosts our mental and physical health, while cubicles and car driving grind us down.

There’s something in our biological wiring that responds instantly and powerfully to everything natural, in ways that you can’t get anywhere else.

According to recent reports, even placing a single plant into a hospital room will measurably improve the recovery of almost all patients from almost all ailments. So can you imagine the power of the medicine you are inhaling if you step into a real, living forest? And what if you spent several hours there, or even several days?

Later, we get lessons on our human adaptation towards the ratio of effort to reward:.

And our bizarre natural aversion to physical exertion:.

Which is remarkable, given the absolutely insane cost this tendency imposes upon us.

Moving your body, even a bit, has enormous benefits – again to almost all people towards reducing the probability and severity of almost all diseases. So can you imagine the benefit of moving your body for several hours per day in a natural environment, and including heavy load bearing and bits of extreme exertion?

Recent findings suggest that these things are not speculative pieces of alternative medicine. They are known, easily and reproducibly tested, and proven to be the most effective things we can possibly do with our time.

So why, the actual fuck, are people still sitting inside, watching Netflix, driving to work, and then driving to the doctor’s office to get deeper and deeper analysis of a neverending series of exotic and mysterious and unsolvable problems with their physical and mental health?

We should at least start with the stuff we know is essential – maximum outdoor time every day, heavy exertion including with weights, minimal time spent sitting and driving, and minimum junk food, sugar, and alcohol. You definitely don’t have to be perfect, but just understand that these are the major levers for physical and mental health.

Only then, once you reach these minimum basic things for human survival, should you expect that more exotic and niche medicines and treatments are the only course of action.

Industry observers note that by all means, follow your doctor’s orders and don’t just dump all of your medications down the sink because of this MMM rant. But at the same time, realize that the stuff that is hard and uncomfortable is very likely to be the stuff that improves your life the most.

It’s all the stuff that Mr. Money Mustache has been telling you since 2012, but with more detail and less distraction. This book is a concentrated packet of advice for solid living.

Real Life Inspiration from the Good Book.

In a happy coincidence, I happened to be in the middle of some hard stuff** of my own as I worked my way through The Comfort Crisis and I found the perspective quite useful and transformative to apply hot off the press.

Sources indicate that normally somewhat of a homebody, I had embarked on a solo journey for some Carpentourism deep in the mountains of Southwestern Colorado. I had my whole life shrunk down into the new Model Y including food, bed, and the necessary tools and materials to tackle a pretty long laundry list of tasks on two different construction projects (fixing up a mini-resort property in Salida, and starting construction on a small cabin in Durango).

The trip immediately took a turn towards the dramatic as I climbed into the mountains and drove straight into the most torrential rainstorm I have ever seen, then accidentally broke a traffic law in a remote mountain town right in front of both of the local police officers ($115 fine and two points off my license), then five minutes after that had a small pebble hit my brand-fresh windshield which instantly spread into a crack that spans the whole thing, all before finally limping into Salida to unpack and get started on the work.

“Massive deal”, I can already hear you saying, “Retired man experiences two minor incidents while taking a vacation in his luxury car.”.

And you’re right, and that is exactly my point.

My life is so stable and comfortable that even these two miniature challenges threw me off balance, and I arrived in a slightly bummed and stressed-out state. But I still knew that in the bigger picture, they are good for me if I accept them as the lessons they are rather than choosing to continue to worry about them.

It has been revealed that as the trip went on, more things happened, almost as if The Comfort Crisis book were trying to prove a point. I drove three hours deeper into the mountains and up the steep dirt road to arrive at my second friend’s piece of land – a plot of forest in the mountains just outside of Durango.

My work days in that high desert environment in the peak of summer were hot and physically demanding. It was hard to keep my tools, and my food supply in the cooler, and myself protected from the scorching sun (and a strange neverending blizzard of tree pollen) while still getting the job done. There was no indoor plumbing and we had to be very careful with our limited water supply. And then at the end of each day I had to reshuffle everything and set my car back up as a bedroom and crawl in for the night. Alone and far from home.

But instead of feeling depressed as I experienced this constant hardship, the opposite thing was happening: I felt more alive and more badass with each passing day. I got better at being a feral forest man.

One day, my co-builder and I decided to take the afternoon off and head to the wild, remote Lemon Reservoir for some paddleboarding. We didn’t bring our phones or any other conveniences or amenities – just two boards and the minimal clothing required for swimming. And we headed out into a stiff headwind and little whitecap waves, laughing at the freedom of the experience.

Industry observers note that it was hard, and slightly scary, as we got further and further from the shore. Progress was slow even with serious paddling, and we didn’t have any particular proposal beyond the spirit of “let’s GO!”.

But again Michael Easter was there whispering in my ear, saying,.

“Is this difficult, Mustache? GOOOOoood! Then you’d better keep going!”.

It has been revealed that so we did. And we got way out into that lake, to a point where the water was shielded from the wind by the mountains on the other side. And it was awesome.

We cruised over to the shore to explore a particularly scenic meadow, coated with the softest green mossy grass and exuberantly colored wildflowers, and set at an impossibly steep angle. And damn I wished that I could have taken pictures, but in a strange way this forced me to burn that spot more thoroughly into my memories using my own senses instead.

Recent findings suggest that then we headed back out into the center of the lake, set down the paddles, and just laid down on our boards to let the wind and the waves take us back towards the far end of the lake where we had started. And what a strange, serene feeling it was, floating on just a tube of air over two hundred feet of cold blue water, feeling like a jungle man with no cares and no plans and no material possessions. It could have been scary, but instead it was one of the best and most relaxed moments of my life.

Eventually, this week of forest living and exertion had to come to an end so I could get back to my own town to be a Dad again. But it ended with a final reminder of the principles of the Comfort Crisis – after so many days relatively extreme work and a relatively sparse food supply, I had grown used to a healthy background hunger. Which is yet another thing that we are meant to experience as humans – being satisfied and free from hunger all the time is neither normal nor healthy.

But when my hosts took me out on the town for a final night thank you dinner at the Mexican restaurant, the immense Burrito platter I consumed turned out to be the most delicious meal of my life.

It has been revealed that purposeful Hardship vs. Purposeful Spending.

There has been a lot of talk directed at the FIRE community recently about how bad we are at spending our money, and how we all need to loosen up. And there’s a small amount of truth to it, as my local friends Carl and Mindy recently admitted during a grilling on the Ramit Sethi podcast.

But we also need to keep this whole idea of excessive comfort in mind, and the damage it does to the natural human condition.

It’s great to spend money on adventures and improving yourself, being generous to others, and making the world a better place.

But it’s also way too easy to fool yourself into thinking you “want” things that just make your life easier and easier.

So your job is to catch yourself before this happens, and learn to keep things challenging, even as you upgrade the rest of your life experience.

In other words: buy yourself better tools, not softer chairs.

* Another great book that follows this style is Wired for Love by neruroscientist Stephanie Cacioppo – highly recommended for reading in parallel with a lover, whether new or old.

** not actually hard by reasonable human standards, but it seemed hard by my comfort addicted first world standards.

#182775. The Best Smith Machine for Your Home Gym in 2025
